title: A Cross-Cell-Type Atlas of Biomolecular Condensate Material States and Their Emergent Control of Gene Expression Noise
abstract:
Biomolecular condensates (10–500 nm substructures within micron-scale droplets) exhibit emergent material properties—viscosity, elasticity, percolation, and multiphase organization—that cannot be predicted from individual protein/RNA components. This project will test the hypothesis that condensate “material state” is a mesoscale emergent variable that systematically tunes transcriptional bursting and cell-to-cell gene expression noise across cell types and perturbations.

We will synthesize publicly available datasets that jointly report (i) condensate composition and disorder features (UniProt, Pfam, MobiDB, DisProt; LLPS/LLPT databases such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS), (ii) condensate morphology and dynamics from imaging repositories (Image Data Resource/IDR, BioImage Archive, Cell Image Library; published FRAP time-series where available), (iii) subcellular localization and puncta statistics from the Human Protein Atlas (immunofluorescence), (iv) single-cell RNA-seq and multiome measurements capturing transcriptional variability (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, GEO; scATAC where available), and (v) perturbation signatures affecting phase behavior (LINCS L1000; CRISPR screens in DepMap where linked to condensate regulators).

Analytically, we will build a unified latent-variable model that maps composition/disorder/sequence grammars and imaging-derived mesoscale features (puncta size distributions, coarsening kinetics proxies, FRAP recovery parameters) onto a low-dimensional “material state manifold.” We will then connect that manifold to emergent transcriptional outcomes using hierarchical Bayesian models of bursting (inferring burst size/frequency from scRNA distributions), and causal discovery on perturbation datasets to identify regulators that shift condensates between states. Deep learning segmentation will standardize puncta calling across imaging sources; meta-analysis will harmonize batch effects and imaging modalities.

Expected insights include: (1) whether distinct condensate classes (nucleoli subcompartments, speckles, stress granules, P-bodies) occupy conserved regions of the material-state manifold across cell types; (2) which sequence grammars and interaction motifs predict transitions between liquid-like and gel-like substructures at 10–1000 nm; and (3) how these mesoscale states correlate with gene expression noise, enabling mechanistic hypotheses for robustness vs. plasticity.

This requires team science because it integrates polymer physics, image analysis, statistical genomics, and protein biophysics; no single lab typically spans high-throughput bioimage mining, scRNA noise modeling, and LLPS sequence/interaction theory. NCEMS support is essential for convening domain experts, creating open pipelines for condensate feature extraction, and producing a community resource: an open, reproducible atlas linking condensate mesoscale material states to emergent gene regulatory phenotypes.

title: Emergent Membrane Curvature Codes: Synthesizing Cryo-ET, Proteomics, and Lipidomics to Predict Organelle Contact Site Morphologies
abstract:
Membrane contact sites (MCS) between organelles are mesoscale structures (10–50 nm gaps; 50–500 nm lateral extents) whose emergent curvature, tether spacing, and protein crowding enable lipid exchange and signaling. The core emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of tethers, scaffolds, and lipids generates stable, functionally specific contact morphologies that are not inferable from single tether proteins.

We will synthesize existing public datasets spanning structure, composition, and function: (i) cryo-electron tomography subtomogram averages and annotations of ER–mitochondria, ER–PM, ER–endosome contacts (EMPIAR, EMDB; published tomograms with segmentation), (ii) proximity labeling and contact-site proteomes (BioID/APEX datasets in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) organelle-resolved lipidomics and membrane composition (LIPID MAPS, Metabolomics Workbench; published organelle fraction lipidomics), (iv) protein structures and predicted complexes for tethers and curvature generators (PDB, AlphaFold DB, EBI Complex Portal), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting contacts (DepMap CRISPR screens; SGD for yeast; MGI for mouse cell lines where applicable).

We will develop a multiscale inference framework that predicts mesoscale contact morphology from molecular components. First, we will extract quantitative geometry from cryo-ET (gap width distributions, curvature tensors, tether density estimates) using standardized segmentation and geometric morphometrics. Second, we will map proteome/lipidome composition to physical parameters (spontaneous curvature, bending rigidity proxies, crowding pressure) using coarse-grained biophysical models. Third, we will train graph neural networks that integrate tether interaction graphs (from structures/predicted interfaces) with lipid composition features to predict observed morphotypes. Finally, we will test whether specific “curvature codes” (combinations of lipid species and tether architectures) generalize across organisms and contact types.

Expected outcomes: (1) a taxonomy of MCS morphotypes grounded in quantitative geometry; (2) predictive rules linking lipid unsaturation, sterol content, and tether oligomerization to emergent curvature and spacing; (3) identification of minimal sets of components sufficient to produce particular morphologies; and (4) hypotheses for why some contacts are robust to perturbations while others switch states.

The work is inherently transdisciplinary: cryo-ET experts, lipidomics/proteomics analysts, structural biologists, and membrane physicists must align data standards and models. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation of heterogeneous datasets, shared open pipelines for geometry extraction and model fitting, and training for trainees in both quantitative imaging and biophysical machine learning. All code, derived features, and models will be released openly to seed community-scale predictive cell biology of mesoscale contact sites.

title: Mesoscale Cytoskeletal Percolation: A Synthesis of Actin/Microtubule Network Architecture and Emergent Intracellular Transport Efficiency
abstract:
Intracellular transport emerges from the collective mesoscale organization of actin and microtubule networks (10–1000 nm filament spacing, crosslinking, and branching) rather than from individual motors or filaments. The emergent phenomenon of interest is percolation-like connectivity and anisotropy in composite cytoskeletal networks that governs cargo routing, traffic jams, and robustness to perturbations.

We will synthesize public datasets across imaging, proteomics, and trafficking phenotypes: (i) super-resolution and expansion microscopy images of actin/microtubules and associated proteins (BioImage Archive, IDR; published STORM/SIM/ExM datasets), (ii) live-cell single-particle tracking of vesicles/organelles (Cell Tracking Challenge datasets; published tracking data in Zenodo/GEO supplements), (iii) proteomics of cytoskeletal fractions and crosslinkers (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) single-cell transcriptomics for cytoskeletal regulators across cell types (Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens), and (v) perturbation screens affecting trafficking (DepMap CRISPR, genome-wide RNAi datasets; LINCS signatures for cytoskeletal drugs).

Computationally, we will build a standardized pipeline to reconstruct mesoscale network graphs from images: filament segmentation, orientation fields, junction detection, and estimation of mesh size and crosslink density. We will compute graph-theoretic and statistical physics descriptors (giant component size, betweenness centrality, anisotropy order parameters, percolation thresholds) and relate them to transport metrics derived from tracking (mean squared displacement regimes, directional persistence, stop-and-go statistics). A key methodological innovation is a multiscale “network-to-transport” emulator that predicts transport efficiency from network descriptors using physics-informed machine learning, enabling cross-dataset generalization.

The central hypothesis is that cells occupy constrained regions of a universal phase diagram for composite network organization, and that transitions between phases (e.g., isotropic mesh to aligned bundles; microtubule-dominant highways to actin-dominant cages) correspond to sharp changes in emergent transport behavior. We will test whether these phase boundaries are conserved across cell types and whether specific regulators (crosslinkers, severing enzymes, nucleators) move cells along predictable trajectories in this diagram.

Expected insights include mechanistic explanations for why certain cell types exhibit robust long-range transport despite noisy molecular composition, and how mesoscale architecture buffers or amplifies perturbations. The project requires team science: computer vision for filament reconstruction, statistical physics for percolation modeling, cell biology for interpretation, and data integration for harmonizing diverse imaging modalities. NCEMS support is needed to convene these communities, curate benchmark datasets, and deliver open, reproducible tools and an atlas linking cytoskeletal mesoscale states to emergent transport phenotypes.

title: Emergent Chromatin Nanodomain Topology: Integrating Hi-C, Super-Resolution Imaging, and Epigenomics to Explain Cell-Type-Specific Gene Regulation
abstract:
Chromatin forms mesoscale nanodomains (50–300 nm) whose collective folding and compartmentalization produce emergent regulatory behaviors—enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting—that cannot be inferred from individual nucleosome modifications. This project will synthesize 3D genome conformation and imaging data to test whether a small set of mesoscale topological motifs explains cell-type-specific gene regulation across mammals.

We will integrate publicly available datasets: (i) population and single-cell Hi-C / Micro-C maps (4D Nucleome, GEO, ENCODE), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed DNA FISH imaging of chromatin domains (4DN data portal, BioImage Archive; Oligopaint datasets), (iii) epigenomic marks and accessibility (ENCODE ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq; Roadmap Epigenomics), (iv) transcriptional outputs (single-cell RNA-seq from Human Cell Atlas; nascent transcription where available), and (v) structural constraints from nucleosome and chromatin fiber models (PDB where relevant; polymer simulation benchmarks).

Methodologically, we will create a joint inference framework that maps between contact matrices and physical 3D domain geometries. We will (1) infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction strengths from Hi-C/Micro-C using multi-resolution community detection; (2) calibrate polymer models with imaging-derived distance distributions to resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions; (3) learn a “motif dictionary” of recurrent mesoscale folding patterns (e.g., loop clusters, rosettes, compartment microdomains) using unsupervised representation learning that ingests both contact and imaging features; and (4) link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes—bursting parameters, enhancer responsiveness, and lineage stability—using hierarchical models across cell types.

The hypothesis is that despite molecular diversity, chromatin nanodomain topology falls into a limited set of mesoscale motifs whose combinations predict regulatory capacity and noise. We will test whether developmental transitions correspond to motif switching, and whether disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially disrupt specific motifs rather than individual loops.

Expected outputs include: a cross-cell-type atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs, quantitative relationships between motif composition and transcriptional variability, and open tools for jointly analyzing Hi-C and imaging. This synthesis requires collaboration among genome informaticians, polymer physicists, microscopy experts, and statistical modelers; no single lab typically has access to and expertise across these modalities. NCEMS working group support is essential for harmonizing standards, building reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to bridge 3D genomics and quantitative imaging under open-science practices.

title: Protein Crowding as an Emergent Mesoscale Regulator: A Pan-Proteome Synthesis of Cytoplasmic Viscosity, Diffusion, and Reaction Rates
abstract:
Cells exhibit emergent mesoscale physical properties—effective viscosity, anomalous diffusion, and spatially heterogeneous crowding—arising from collective protein/RNA concentrations at 10–1000 nm scales. These properties shape signaling and metabolism but are not predictable from individual macromolecules. This project will test whether crowding-related emergent parameters can be predicted from proteome composition and subcellular organization across organisms and conditions.

We will synthesize: (i) quantitative proteomics and absolute protein copy numbers (ProteomeXchange, PaxDB), (ii) subcellular localization and abundance maps (Human Protein Atlas; spatial proteomics datasets such as hyperLOPIT in PRIDE), (iii) measurements of diffusion and viscosity from fluorescence correlation spectroscopy, single-particle tracking, and FRAP compiled from public repositories and literature supplements (IDR/BioImage Archive; curated datasets), (iv) metabolomics that influences osmotic/crowding states (Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) structural/biophysical properties of proteins (PDB, AlphaFold DB; predicted disorder from MobiDB; oligomerization from Complex Portal).

We will construct mesoscale “crowding fields” by combining spatial proteomics with protein size/shape estimates (from structures/predictions) to estimate excluded volume and soft interaction potentials in different compartments. We will fit these fields to observed diffusion/viscosity measurements using Bayesian calibration and coarse-grained physical models (e.g., obstruction scaling, fractional Brownian motion). Machine learning models will predict diffusion regimes for probe classes (enzymes, ribosomes, signaling proteins) given local proteome composition and interaction propensity.

Key questions: Do cells maintain conserved crowding setpoints in specific compartments (nucleoplasm vs cytosol) despite large proteome changes? Which protein classes (ribosomal proteins, chaperones, intrinsically disordered proteins) disproportionately control emergent viscosity? Can we predict condition-dependent shifts (stress, cell cycle, differentiation) in mesoscale diffusion landscapes from omics alone?

Expected insights include a quantitative, cross-species map linking proteome composition to emergent physical states, and identification of “crowding hubs” whose abundance changes re-tune global reaction kinetics. The project enables reinterpretation of many phenotypes (e.g., slowed signaling under stress) as consequences of mesoscale physical state changes.

This requires team science integrating quantitative proteomics, soft-matter physics, microscopy-based biophysics, and statistical learning, plus substantial data curation across heterogeneous measurement types. NCEMS support is needed to coordinate community standards for reporting diffusion/viscosity, build open databases of calibrated measurements, and deliver reproducible pipelines and training modules for a new generation of data-savvy biophysical cell biologists.

title: Emergent Ribosome Assembly Landscapes: Integrating Cryo-EM Intermediates, rRNA Processing Maps, and Proteomics to Explain Assembly Robustness
abstract:
Ribosome biogenesis involves mesoscale ribonucleoprotein intermediates (20–30 nm) that undergo coordinated folding, processing, and factor exchange. The emergent phenomenon is robust, directional assembly arising from collective interactions among rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and dozens of assembly factors—behavior not deducible from any single component. This project will synthesize structural and functional datasets to infer universal principles governing assembly pathway robustness and failure modes.

We will integrate: (i) cryo-EM structures of ribosome assembly intermediates and associated factors (EMDB, PDB), (ii) time-resolved rRNA processing and modification maps (RNA-seq and specialized datasets in GEO/SRA; MODOMICS for modifications), (iii) quantitative proteomics of assembly factors and ribosomal proteins under perturbations (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) genetic interaction and essentiality data for assembly factors (BioGRID, DepMap; yeast genetic interaction networks), and (v) subcellular localization/imaging of nucleolar subcompartments (Human Protein Atlas; IDR datasets).

We will build a unified “assembly state graph” where nodes are structural intermediates (from cryo-EM) and edges represent transitions constrained by rRNA processing events and factor binding/unbinding. Using probabilistic graphical models and energy landscape concepts, we will infer transition probabilities and identify bottlenecks. Comparative analysis across bacteria, yeast, and human will reveal conserved vs lineage-specific modules. We will also apply network controllability analysis to identify minimal sets of factors that steer assembly away from dead-end states.

Hypotheses: (1) assembly robustness emerges from redundant, partially ordered modules that buffer factor loss; (2) specific mesoscale nucleolar subcompartments correspond to distinct regions of the assembly state graph; and (3) disease mutations in ribosomopathies disproportionately affect transitions with low redundancy, explaining tissue-specific vulnerability.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of assembly intermediates aligned to processing timelines, quantitative identification of fragile transitions, and mechanistic explanations for why some perturbations cause global collapse while others are compensated. Methodological advances include pipelines to harmonize heterogeneous cryo-EM intermediate annotations and to integrate structural states with sequencing-based processing data.

This project requires collaboration among cryo-EM structural biologists, RNA processing experts, network scientists, and disease geneticists, and it depends entirely on integrating numerous public datasets beyond any single lab’s scope. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open workflows, and trainee-led hackathons to produce reusable resources for understanding emergent mesoscale assembly in RNP machines.

title: Mesoscale Signaling Microclusters as Emergent Computation: A Synthesis of Immune Receptor Imaging, Phosphoproteomics, and Single-Cell Responses
abstract:
Immune receptors form mesoscale microclusters (50–300 nm) at the plasma membrane that act as emergent computational units, integrating ligand binding, mechanical forces, and feedback to produce switch-like or graded activation. The emergent phenomenon is that collective receptor organization and kinase/phosphatase partitioning yields signaling behaviors not predictable from receptor–ligand affinity alone.

We will synthesize: (i) TCR/BCR and Fc receptor super-resolution and TIRF imaging datasets with cluster statistics (IDR, BioImage Archive; published single-molecule localization microscopy datasets), (ii) phosphoproteomics time courses following receptor stimulation (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iii) single-cell functional readouts (CyTOF and flow cytometry in ImmPort; scRNA-seq activation time courses in GEO), (iv) ligand affinity/kinetics and epitope data (IEDB; structural complexes in PDB), and (v) perturbation datasets for kinases, phosphatases, and cytoskeletal regulators (DepMap; LINCS small-molecule perturbations).

Analytically, we will develop a multiscale model linking microcluster architecture to downstream phosphorylation and transcription. Computer vision and point-process statistics will quantify cluster size distributions, lifetimes, and nanoscale colocalization of signaling proteins. We will integrate these features with phosphoproteomic trajectories via dynamical systems identification (sparse regression / SINDy) and with single-cell outcomes using mixture models to capture heterogeneous activation states. A key goal is to infer whether there exist universal “microcluster motifs” (e.g., kinase-rich cores with phosphatase-exclusion shells) that correspond to distinct emergent response modes.

Hypotheses: (1) microcluster morphology encodes a mesoscale “gain control” that determines sensitivity vs specificity; (2) cytoskeletal coupling shifts microcluster systems between excitable and bistable regimes; and (3) disease-associated variants in signaling proteins act by altering partitioning into clusters rather than changing catalytic rates.

Expected insights include predictive relationships between nanoscale organization and functional immune outcomes, a cross-study standardized microcluster feature set, and mechanistic explanations for disparate experimental results in the literature. This requires team science spanning immunology, quantitative imaging, proteomics, and dynamical modeling, plus significant synthesis to harmonize stimulation protocols and imaging modalities.

NCEMS support is essential to convene communities, build open pipelines for microcluster quantification, and create an openly accessible benchmark dataset and modeling toolkit. Trainees will gain cross-disciplinary training in image analysis, omics integration, and reproducible computational immunology.

title: Emergent Mitochondrial Cristae Morphodynamics: Integrating Cryo-ET, Live Imaging, and Proteogenomics to Explain Bioenergetic Plasticity
abstract:
Mitochondrial cristae are mesoscale membrane folds (20–100 nm curvature radii; 10–30 nm junctions) whose collective organization determines respiratory efficiency and signaling. The emergent phenomenon is that cristae architecture—junction density, lamellar vs tubular balance, and local protein crowding—produces nonlinear changes in bioenergetic output not predictable from individual OXPHOS complexes.

We will synthesize public datasets: (i) cryo-ET reconstructions and segmentations of cristae across conditions and organisms (EMPIAR, EMDB), (ii) live-cell imaging of mitochondrial dynamics and cristae reporters where available (IDR/BioImage Archive; Mitochondria Dynamics datasets), (iii) proteomics/phosphoproteomics of mitochondrial fractions and MICOS/OPA1/ATP synthase oligomers (PRIDE), (iv) genomics and transcriptomics for mitochondrial-shaping genes (GTEx, ENCODE; scRNA-seq atlases), and (v) functional readouts of respiration (public Seahorse datasets and compiled literature values; gene perturbation phenotypes in DepMap).

We will quantify mesoscale cristae geometry from cryo-ET via curvature analysis, junction graph extraction, and topology measures (surface genus, connectivity). We will integrate these with proteomic abundance of shaping complexes and with genetic perturbation effects using causal inference and multi-task learning. Physics-informed models of membrane elasticity and protein-induced curvature will be calibrated to explain observed morphotypes and predict transitions.

Central questions: Are there conserved cristae “architectural states” across cell types that correspond to distinct metabolic regimes? Which combinations of MICOS components, ATP synthase dimerization, and OPA1 processing drive state transitions? Can we explain why similar proteomic changes yield different functional outcomes in different tissues as a consequence of mesoscale geometry constraints?

Expected insights include an atlas of cristae architectural states, quantitative links between shaping complex stoichiometry and emergent cristae topology, and mechanistic hypotheses for mitochondrial diseases where morphology and function decouple. Methodological advances will include open-source tools for extracting standardized geometric descriptors from tomograms.

The project demands collaboration between cryo-ET experts, mitochondrial biologists, membrane physicists, and machine learning scientists, and requires extensive synthesis of heterogeneous structural and omics data beyond a single lab’s capability. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, open workflows, and trainee training in quantitative 3D ultrastructure analysis and integrative modeling.

title: Mesoscale Assembly of Viral Replication Compartments: A Cross-Virus Synthesis of Host Factor Recruitment and Emergent Replication Efficiency
abstract:
Many viruses create mesoscale replication compartments (100–1000 nm membraneless inclusions or membrane-bound organelles) that concentrate viral and host factors. The emergent phenomenon is that collective compartment organization yields replication efficiencies and immune evasion strategies not predictable from individual viral proteins. This project will ask whether replication compartments share universal mesoscale design principles across unrelated viruses.

We will synthesize: (i) viral replication compartment imaging datasets (electron microscopy and fluorescence) from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR, spanning RNA viruses (coronaviruses, flaviviruses) and DNA viruses (herpesviruses), (ii) host–virus protein interaction networks (IntAct, BioGRID, VirHostNet), (iii) CRISPR and RNAi screens for host dependency factors (DepMap viral screens; published screens in GEO/SRA), (iv) viral and host transcriptomic responses (GEO; single-cell infection atlases where available), and (v) structural data for viral scaffold proteins and host recruited complexes (PDB, AlphaFold DB).

We will develop a comparative mesoscale compartment feature framework: size distributions, internal subcompartmentalization, proximity to organelles, and dynamics proxies. Using network embedding and community detection on host–virus interactomes, we will identify recurrent host modules (e.g., RNA metabolism, membrane trafficking, stress granule components) recruited into compartments. We will then relate these modules to compartment morphotypes and to replication phenotypes (viral titers/replication markers from public datasets) using multi-level regression and causal graph methods.

Hypotheses: (1) replication compartments implement convergent mesoscale strategies—phase separation, membrane curvature scaffolding, or hybrid forms—to optimize reaction kinetics and shield nucleic acids; (2) the emergent efficiency depends on a small number of host module recruitments that act as “mesoscale organizers”; and (3) antiviral perturbations that disrupt mesoscale organization (rather than single enzymes) provide broad-spectrum leverage.

Expected insights include a cross-virus taxonomy of replication compartment architectures, identification of conserved host mesoscale organizers, and predictive models linking host factor modules to compartment type and replication success. Deliverables will include open compartment feature datasets and interoperable pipelines for image and network integration.

This requires team science across virology, quantitative imaging, network biology, and statistical modeling, and it relies entirely on integrating diverse public datasets. NCEMS support is crucial to coordinate cross-virus data harmonization, establish open standards for compartment annotation, and train trainees in integrative, reproducible computational virology focused on emergent mesoscale organization.

title: Emergent Cell Wall Nanomechanics: Synthesizing Fungal and Plant Cell Wall Composition, Ultrastructure, and Growth Patterns
abstract:
Cell walls are mesoscale composite materials (10–500 nm fibril bundles, crosslinks, and pores) whose emergent mechanical properties enable growth, morphogenesis, and stress resistance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polysaccharide architecture produces nonlinear stiffness, anisotropy, and fracture behavior not predictable from monomer composition. This project will synthesize multi-omics and imaging data to uncover universal principles of cell wall nanocomposite design in plants and fungi.

We will integrate: (i) cell wall compositional datasets (glycomics and carbohydrate-active enzyme annotations from CAZy; polysaccharide composition in Metabolomics Workbench and literature-derived datasets), (ii) solid-state NMR and scattering data where publicly available (BMRB; published SAXS/WAXS datasets), (iii) AFM nanomechanics maps and electron microscopy of wall ultrastructure (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (iv) transcriptomics of wall biosynthesis during growth and stress (GEO; Arabidopsis eFP, fungal expression atlases), and (v) mutant/perturbation phenotypes affecting morphology (TAIR, SGD, FungiDB; high-content imaging screens).

Analytically, we will build a mesoscale structure–property model linking polymer composition and enzyme expression to ultrastructural descriptors (fibril orientation, bundling, pore size distributions) and to mechanical outputs (Young’s modulus maps, viscoelastic parameters). We will use Bayesian meta-analysis to harmonize AFM protocols and machine learning to infer ultrastructure from indirect measurements (NMR/scattering) when imaging is absent. Network models of CAZyme co-expression will be linked to predicted architectural states.

Key questions: Do plant and fungal walls occupy shared regions of a mesoscale “design space” balancing stiffness and extensibility? Which crosslink motifs (e.g., lignin–cellulose coupling vs chitin–glucan branching) create emergent anisotropic growth? Can we predict growth patterns and failure modes under stress from mesoscale architecture rather than gene lists?

Expected insights include a cross-kingdom atlas of wall mesoscale architectures, identification of convergent nanocomposite strategies, and mechanistic hypotheses for how cells tune growth directionality by reorganizing nanoscale fibrils. The project will generate open tools for quantifying wall ultrastructure and mechanical heterogeneity.

This synthesis requires plant biologists, mycologists, polymer physicists, and computational image analysts, and depends on integrating heterogeneous public datasets beyond any single lab. NCEMS support enables coordinated curation, shared modeling infrastructure, and trainee training in quantitative biomaterials analysis under open science principles.

title: Mesoscale Proteasome and Autophagy Hub Organization: Integrating Spatial Proteomics, Imaging, and Ubiquitinome Data to Explain Proteostasis Emergence
abstract:
Proteostasis emerges from mesoscale organization of degradation hubs—proteasome-rich microdomains, aggresomes, and autophagy initiation sites (50–1000 nm)—that coordinate substrate selection, sequestration, and clearance. The emergent phenomenon is that collective spatial organization and phase-like sequestration yields system-level robustness to misfolded proteins, not predictable from individual E3 ligases or proteases.

We will synthesize: (i) spatial proteomics identifying proteasome/autophagy component localization (Human Protein Atlas; hyperLOPIT and proximity labeling datasets in PRIDE), (ii) ubiquitinomics and proteome turnover datasets (PRIDE; ubiquitin linkage-specific studies), (iii) bioimaging of aggresomes, p62 bodies, autophagosome markers, and proteasome foci (IDR/BioImage Archive), (iv) genetic perturbation screens for proteostasis regulators (DepMap; CRISPR screens for aggregation/toxicity), and (v) disease datasets with proteostasis failure signatures (AMP-AD proteomics; ALS/FTD proteomics and transcriptomics in GEO).

We will quantify mesoscale hub features from images (number, size, spatial distribution relative to organelles) using standardized segmentation and spatial statistics. We will integrate these with ubiquitinome features (linkage composition, substrate networks) and with turnover rates to infer how hub organization modulates degradation flux. Dynamical modeling will connect hub formation kinetics to emergent outcomes such as threshold-like aggregation onset. Multi-omic factor analysis will identify latent “proteostasis states” shared across stresses and diseases.

Hypotheses: (1) cells switch between distinct mesoscale proteostasis strategies—distributed microdomains vs centralized aggresome routing—depending on crowding and ubiquitin network topology; (2) specific ubiquitin linkage patterns bias substrates toward particular hubs; and (3) neurodegenerative disease signatures reflect a shift in mesoscale hub organization rather than solely changes in expression.

Expected insights include a unified atlas of proteostasis hub architectures across cell types and stresses, mechanistic links between ubiquitin network structure and mesoscale sequestration, and candidate mesoscale biomarkers of early proteostasis collapse.

This requires team science across imaging, ubiquitin biochemistry, systems biology, and neurodegeneration, with heavy emphasis on data harmonization and reproducible pipelines. NCEMS support is needed to curate dispersed datasets, develop open standards for hub annotation, and train trainees in integrative analysis of spatial proteomics and bioimage-derived mesoscale features.

title: Emergent Bacterial Microcompartment Design Rules: Synthesizing Genomes, Structures, and Metabolic Flux to Predict Organelle-Like Function
abstract:
Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are proteinaceous organelles (50–300 nm) whose emergent permeability and enzyme colocalization enable metabolic pathways that would be inefficient or toxic in the cytosol. The emergent phenomenon is that shell protein assembly and pore organization generate selective transport and reaction microenvironments not predictable from individual enzymes.

We will synthesize: (i) BMC gene clusters across bacterial genomes (NCBI RefSeq, IMG; curated BMC databases), (ii) shell protein and encapsulated enzyme structures (PDB, AlphaFold DB), (iii) metabolomics and flux measurements for BMC-associated pathways (Metabolomics Workbench; published 13C flux studies), (iv) cryo-EM structures of intact BMCs and shells (EMDB/EMPIAR), and (v) environmental metadata and phenotypes for host organisms (GOLD database; literature-derived growth phenotypes).

We will build a comparative framework linking genetic composition to mesoscale shell architecture and emergent function. First, we will annotate shell protein families and predict pore properties (charge, diameter, gating motifs) from structures. Second, we will infer likely shell stoichiometries and tessellation patterns using assembly modeling and constraints from cryo-EM. Third, we will integrate pathway enzyme kinetics (from BRENDA) with predicted permeability to simulate emergent metabolite gradients and flux enhancement using reaction–diffusion models. Machine learning will map gene cluster features to predicted organelle performance metrics (toxicity mitigation, flux gain).

Key questions: Are there universal shell “permeability motifs” that recur across unrelated BMC types? How do small changes in pore composition produce emergent switches between retention vs throughput regimes? Can we predict ecological niches where particular BMC designs confer advantage?

Expected insights include design rules for emergent mesoscale selectivity, a taxonomy of BMC architectures linked to metabolic outcomes, and open tools for predicting BMC function from genomes. While synthetic biology implications exist, the project itself uses only public data and focuses on fundamental principles of mesoscale emergence.

This effort requires collaboration among microbiologists, structural biologists, metabolic modelers, and evolutionary bioinformaticians, and depends on integrating large-scale genomic data with structural and metabolic measurements. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open pipelines, and trainee training in multiscale modeling of protein-based organelles.

title: Mesoscale Vesicle Coat Self-Organization: Integrating Structural Proteomics and Imaging to Explain Cargo Selectivity Emergence
abstract:
Vesicle coats (clathrin, COPI, COPII) assemble into mesoscale lattices (50–150 nm vesicles; ~10–20 nm lattice spacing) that generate curvature and select cargo. The emergent phenomenon is that collective lattice geometry and adaptor clustering yields cargo selectivity and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual coat subunits.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of coat assemblies and adaptor complexes (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proteomics of coated vesicles and adaptor interactomes (PRIDE; BioGRID/IntAct interactions), (iii) high-content imaging of trafficking markers and coat puncta (IDR; Cell Painting datasets where relevant), (iv) cargo proteomes and sorting signal annotations (UniProt; curated motif databases), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes for coat/adaptor genes (DepMap; yeast deletion phenotypes in SGD).

We will quantify coat puncta and vesicle size proxies from imaging, and integrate with structural parameters (lattice curvature preferences, binding site densities). Graph-based models will represent adaptor–cargo networks, while physics-informed simulations will connect adaptor clustering to emergent cargo enrichment under constraints of lattice geometry. We will use probabilistic models to infer how adaptor competition and cooperative binding produce sharp cargo sorting thresholds.

Hypotheses: (1) vesicle coats operate near geometric frustration points where small changes in adaptor composition shift vesicle size and cargo repertoire; (2) emergent cargo selectivity is driven by mesoscale clustering of adaptors into subdomains within the coat; and (3) disease mutations in trafficking genes often act by altering mesoscale lattice parameters rather than abolishing binding.

Expected insights include a unified model connecting coat architecture to cargo selection across pathways, identification of conserved mesoscale adaptor subdomain motifs, and open resources linking structural and imaging-derived coat features.

This synthesis requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, trafficking cell biology, and computational modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize disparate datasets, build open analysis pipelines, and train trainees to integrate structure, networks, and bioimage-derived mesoscale phenotypes under reproducible open science.

title: Emergent Nuclear Pore Selectivity at the Mesoscale: A Synthesis of FG-Nup Disorder, Transport Kinetics, and NPC Ultrastructure
abstract:
Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) are ~100 nm assemblies whose central FG-nucleoporin (FG-Nup) network forms a selective permeability barrier—an emergent property arising from collective polymer behavior rather than any single FG repeat. This project will synthesize structural, sequence, and transport datasets to test how mesoscale organization of FG-Nups encodes selectivity and transport modes across species and cell states.

We will integrate: (i) NPC structural data from cryo-ET and cryo-EM (EMDB/EMPIAR; PDB for scaffold subcomplexes), (ii) FG-Nup sequences, disorder annotations, and repeat grammars (UniProt, MobiDB, DisProt), (iii) quantitative transport kinetics measurements (single-molecule transport, FRAP, import/export rates) from published datasets and supplements, (iv) proteomics of NPC composition and post-translational modifications (PRIDE), and (v) genetic perturbation phenotypes affecting transport (SGD; DepMap; disease variant databases for nucleoporins).

We will build a multiscale model linking FG-Nup polymer physics to observed transport selectivity. Sequence-derived features (FG motif spacing, charge patterning) will parameterize coarse-grained polymer simulations and analytical theories (brush/gels). Structural constraints from NPC ultrastructure will define boundary conditions. We will then fit model predictions to transport kinetics via Bayesian inference, enabling estimation of emergent parameters such as mesh size, cohesive interaction strength, and heterogeneity across the pore.

Key questions: Do different cell types or organisms achieve similar selectivity via distinct FG-Nup sequence grammars (many-to-one mapping)? Are there discrete “barrier states” corresponding to transport regimes (fast/slow, size cutoff shifts) modulated by phosphorylation or composition changes? Can disease-associated mutations be explained as shifts in emergent barrier parameters rather than loss of specific interactions?

Expected insights include a comparative atlas of FG-Nup grammars mapped to inferred barrier states, quantitative links between ultrastructure and transport, and open tools for fitting polymer-based NPC models to data.

This effort requires collaboration among polymer physicists, structural biologists, quantitative microscopists, and computational biologists, and hinges on synthesizing diverse public datasets. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, reproducible modeling workflows, and trainee training at the interface of disordered protein science and mesoscale transport phenomena.

title: Mesoscale Emergence in Bacterial Biofilm Matrix Nanostructure: Integrating Omics, Imaging, and Rheology to Predict Community Robustness
abstract:
Biofilms are stabilized by extracellular matrix (ECM) nanostructures (10–500 nm fibers, pores, and crosslinked networks) whose emergent viscoelasticity and diffusional barriers create antibiotic tolerance and spatial metabolic stratification. The emergent phenomenon is that collective polymer and protein assembly yields community-level robustness not predictable from individual ECM components.

We will synthesize: (i) biofilm imaging datasets including confocal, super-resolution, and electron microscopy of ECM architectures (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) metagenomic and transcriptomic profiles of biofilm communities (NCBI SRA; MG-RAST), (iii) proteomics of ECM and secretomes (PRIDE), (iv) publicly available rheology/viscoelastic measurements and diffusion assays (compiled from literature with open data), and (v) antibiotic susceptibility and perturbation datasets (PATRIC; published screens).

We will extract mesoscale structural descriptors from images (fiber thickness distributions, pore size, network connectivity) using segmentation and graph reconstruction. We will integrate these with ECM composition inferred from omics (polysaccharide synthesis genes, amyloid proteins, eDNA abundance proxies) to build predictive models of emergent rheology and diffusional barrier properties. Reaction–diffusion modeling will connect matrix structure to nutrient/antibiotic penetration and to spatial gene expression patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) diverse biofilms converge on a small set of mesoscale ECM architectures that define mechanical and barrier “states”; (2) community composition influences architecture through modular ECM programs; and (3) transitions between ECM states under stress explain abrupt changes in tolerance.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of ECM mesoscale architectures, mechanistic links between matrix nanostructure and emergent tolerance, and open tools for standardized ECM quantification. The work is purely synthesis-based, leveraging existing datasets to unify previously disconnected measurements.

Team science is required across microbiology, materials science, image analysis, and ecological modeling. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous datasets, establish open standards for ECM feature reporting, and train trainees in integrative analysis of microbial communities and mesoscale biomaterials under open science practices.

title: Emergent Spliceosome Nano-Organization: Integrating RNP Structural States, Proximity Proteomics, and Single-Cell Isoform Variability
abstract:
Pre-mRNA splicing is executed by spliceosomes and associated nuclear speckle substructures at mesoscale dimensions (20–200 nm RNP assemblies; 100–500 nm speckle subdomains). The emergent phenomenon is that collective organization of splicing factors into dynamic assemblies produces cell-type-specific isoform distributions and noise, beyond what individual RNA-binding proteins predict.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-EM structures of spliceosome intermediates (PDB/EMDB), (ii) proximity labeling proteomics of speckles and splicing assemblies (PRIDE), (iii) super-resolution imaging of speckle organization and splicing factor puncta (BioImage Archive/IDR), (iv) long-read and single-cell RNA-seq isoform datasets (ENCODE long-read; GEO; Human Cell Atlas where isoform-resolved methods exist), and (v) perturbation screens of splicing factors (DepMap; CRISPR screens; ClinVar variants for splicing genes).

We will build a multiscale model connecting structural intermediate occupancy and speckle mesoscale organization to isoform outcomes. Image-derived features will quantify speckle subdomain size, factor partitioning, and dynamics proxies. Structural states will be represented as a Markov model of assembly intermediates, parameterized by factor availability from proteomics. We will relate these latent variables to isoform variability using hierarchical models and information-theoretic measures of splicing entropy.

Hypotheses: (1) cells regulate splicing by shifting mesoscale partitioning of factors between speckles and nucleoplasm, altering effective assembly kinetics; (2) specific speckle organizational states correspond to low-entropy (deterministic) vs high-entropy (diverse) isoform programs; and (3) disease mutations increase isoform noise by destabilizing particular intermediate transitions.

Expected insights include an atlas linking speckle mesoscale states to isoform variability across cell types, identification of key factors controlling emergent splicing entropy, and open pipelines for integrating imaging with isoform-resolved transcriptomics.

This requires team science across structural biology, quantitative imaging, transcriptomics, and statistical modeling. NCEMS support is essential for harmonizing disparate data modalities and producing reproducible workflows and training materials enabling trainees to operate across RNP structural biology and single-cell genomics.

title: Mesoscale Organization of Metabolic Enzyme Filaments: A Cross-Species Synthesis of Cytoophidia and Emergent Metabolic Regulation
abstract:
Many metabolic enzymes assemble into mesoscale filaments and bundles (50–1000 nm), such as CTP synthase cytoophidia and IMPDH filaments. The emergent phenomenon is that polymerization changes enzyme kinetics, sequestration, and pathway flux in a nonlinear manner not predictable from monomeric enzyme properties. This project will synthesize imaging, structural, and metabolomic data to uncover universal principles of enzyme filament-based regulation.

We will integrate: (i) fluorescence and electron microscopy datasets showing enzyme filaments across organisms and conditions (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) enzyme structures and filament models (PDB; AlphaFold DB; published helical reconstructions), (iii) metabolomics profiling nucleotide pools and related pathways (Metabolomics Workbench), (iv) transcriptomics and proteomics for enzyme abundance and PTMs (GEO; PRIDE), and (v) perturbation datasets (LINCS for metabolic inhibitors; genetic screens affecting filament formation).

We will quantify filament morphology (length distributions, bundling, subcellular localization) and link these to metabolic state variables (nucleotide ratios, energy stress markers). Using mechanistic modeling, we will compare alternative hypotheses: polymerization as inhibition, activation, or buffering reservoir, and determine which best explains cross-study correlations. We will use phylogenetic comparative methods to test whether filament regulation evolved convergently and whether specific sequence motifs predict polymerization propensity.

Key questions: Are there discrete mesoscale filament “states” corresponding to metabolic regimes (growth, stress, differentiation)? Do filaments act as emergent metabolic capacitors that reduce noise in metabolite levels? Can we predict when filamentation will stabilize vs destabilize pathway flux?

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of enzyme filament states, quantitative links between filament morphology and metabolite homeostasis, and open tools for filament detection and meta-analysis. This synthesis will unify scattered observations into a coherent framework for mesoscale metabolic regulation.

Team science is required across metabolism, structural biology, imaging analysis, and evolutionary genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation of diverse datasets, development of open pipelines, and trainee training in integrative analysis of mesoscale enzyme assemblies and metabolic phenotypes.

title: Emergent Endocytic Pit Nanoscale Heterogeneity: Integrating Single-Molecule Imaging and Proteomics to Explain Uptake Variability
abstract:
Clathrin-mediated endocytosis produces ~100 nm pits whose emergent behavior—variable lifetimes, abortive events, and cargo-dependent maturation—arises from collective assembly of many proteins and membrane mechanics. The emergent phenomenon is nanoscale heterogeneity in pit trajectories that creates cell-to-cell and site-to-site variability in uptake.

We will synthesize: (i) single-molecule and live-cell imaging datasets tracking endocytic proteins and pit lifetimes (IDR/BioImage Archive; published tracking datasets), (ii) proteomics of endocytic complexes and phosphorylation dynamics (PRIDE), (iii) cargo-specific uptake assays and receptor datasets (GEO; literature datasets with quantitative uptake), (iv) membrane lipid composition datasets relevant to endocytosis (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), and (v) perturbation screens for endocytosis regulators (DepMap; yeast endocytosis screens).

We will standardize pit trajectory extraction and build a probabilistic “pit state machine” model capturing transitions among assembly, maturation, scission, and abortive states. We will link state transition probabilities to protein abundance/PTMs and lipid composition using hierarchical Bayesian inference. Unsupervised clustering will identify recurrent mesoscale pit “phenotypes” and relate them to cargo classes.

Hypotheses: (1) emergent uptake variability is governed by a small number of mesoscale control parameters (effective adaptor cooperativity, actin coupling strength, membrane tension proxies) that can be inferred from omics and imaging; (2) different cargos shift pits into distinct dynamical regimes; and (3) cells tune variability (noise) as a functional feature for receptor signaling.

Expected insights include a unified dynamical model explaining why pits with similar molecular parts produce divergent outcomes, and an open atlas of pit phenotypes across conditions. Methodological deliverables will include reproducible pipelines for cross-study trajectory harmonization.

This project requires collaboration among quantitative microscopists, trafficking biologists, proteomics experts, and statisticians. NCEMS support is needed for data curation, development of open standards for reporting trajectories and pit features, and training trainees in integrative modeling of mesoscale membrane remodeling.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of Synaptic Active Zone Nanoclusters: A Synthesis of Proteomics, Super-Resolution Maps, and Functional Plasticity
abstract:
Synaptic active zones contain nanoscale protein nanoclusters (20–200 nm) whose collective arrangement controls neurotransmitter release probability and plasticity. The emergent phenomenon is that mesoscale spatial patterning of channels, scaffolds, and vesicle docking sites produces nonlinear release dynamics not predictable from single protein abundances.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution maps of active zone proteins (STED/PALM datasets in BioImage Archive/IDR), (ii) synaptosome and active zone proteomics across brain regions and conditions (PRIDE; SynProt resources), (iii) electrophysiological and imaging-derived functional measures (paired-pulse ratios, release probability proxies) from public repositories and literature open data, (iv) genetic variant and perturbation data for synaptic proteins (SFARI, ClinVar; mouse phenotyping databases), and (v) developmental single-cell transcriptomics of neuronal types (Allen Brain Atlas; scRNA-seq datasets).

We will quantify nanocluster geometry (cluster size, spacing, co-localization networks) and build spatial point-process models linking organization to release probability. Integrative modeling will connect proteomic stoichiometry to predicted nanoscale architectures using constraints from known structural interactions (PDB/AlphaFold). We will test whether synapses occupy discrete “organizational states” corresponding to functional plasticity modes.

Hypotheses: (1) active zones implement a small set of mesoscale architectures that tune reliability vs flexibility; (2) plasticity involves transitions between these architectures mediated by scaffold phosphorylation and remodeling; and (3) neurodevelopmental disorder variants shift synapses into maladaptive organizational states.

Expected insights include a cross-region atlas of active zone nanoscale architectures, mechanistic links between organization and emergent release dynamics, and open analysis tools for nanocluster quantification and integration with proteomics.

This requires team science across neuroscience, proteomics, quantitative imaging, and spatial statistics, with extensive synthesis across disparate datasets. NCEMS support will enable harmonization, open workflows, and trainee training bridging nanoscale organization and systems-level synaptic function.

title: Emergent Organelle Size Control via Mesoscale Substructure: Integrating Imaging Atlases and Omics to Explain Scaling Laws
abstract:
Organelle size (nucleoli, centrosomes, lysosomes, peroxisomes) is governed by mesoscale substructures—subcompartments, scaffolds, and assembly intermediates (10–1000 nm)—that create emergent scaling laws with cell size and growth state. The emergent phenomenon is that collective assembly dynamics yield robust organelle size distributions across noisy molecular environments.

We will synthesize: (i) large-scale cell imaging atlases with organelle segmentation (Human Protein Atlas Cell Atlas; IDR high-content datasets; Cell Painting), (ii) single-cell transcriptomics and proteomics capturing cell state (Human Cell Atlas; CITE-seq datasets; PRIDE single-cell proteomics where available), (iii) known organelle biogenesis pathways and interaction networks (Reactome, BioGRID), (iv) perturbation datasets affecting organelle size (DepMap; LINCS), and (v) ultrastructural datasets for organelle subcompartments (EMPIAR for selected organelles).

We will extract organelle size distributions and mesoscale texture/substructure features from images (granularity, internal puncta, boundary roughness) and relate them to molecular composition and cell size using scaling analysis and stochastic assembly models (nucleation–growth, coalescence, fragmentation). We will test competing mechanistic models (limiting pool, feedback control, coarsening-limited growth) across organelles and cell types.

Key questions: Are there universal mesoscale control motifs that recur across organelles (e.g., scaffold-limited nucleation, fragmentation-mediated size homeostasis)? Which molecular regulators tune variance vs mean size? Do disease states reflect altered control motifs leading to broader distributions (loss of homeostasis) rather than simple size shifts?

Expected insights include generalized principles of organelle size control grounded in measurable mesoscale features, and open tools for extracting substructure descriptors from public imaging. The project will yield a comparative “organelle scaling atlas” linking size control regimes to molecular networks.

This requires team science across quantitative cell imaging, stochastic modeling, and omics integration. NCEMS support is essential for large-scale data harmonization, development of reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to connect mesoscale organization to emergent cellular-scale phenotypes under open science.

title: Mesoscale Emergence in DNA Damage Repair Foci: Integrating Live Imaging, Proteomics, and 3D Genome Context
abstract:
DNA damage repair foci are mesoscale assemblies (100–1000 nm) where many proteins and chromatin regions co-localize, often with phase-separation-like properties. The emergent phenomenon is that collective recruitment and chromatin reorganization creates threshold responses, pathway choice (HR vs NHEJ), and repair timing not predictable from individual repair factors.

We will synthesize: (i) live-cell imaging datasets of repair foci dynamics (53BP1, RAD51, γH2AX) from IDR/BioImage Archive, including time-lapse series, (ii) proteomics and phosphoproteomics of DNA damage response (DDR) time courses (PRIDE), (iii) 3D genome and chromatin context maps (Hi-C/Micro-C from 4DN; ENCODE epigenomics), (iv) CRISPR screens for DDR genes and pathway choice modifiers (DepMap; published DDR screens), and (v) variant datasets for DDR genes in cancer (TCGA; COSMIC).

We will develop a unified model linking chromatin context and protein network state to mesoscale foci morphodynamics. Imaging analysis will quantify foci nucleation rates, growth/coalescence, and dissolution, extracting mesoscale kinetic parameters. We will integrate these with phosphoproteomic signaling states and with chromatin compartment features at damage-prone loci. Causal inference will identify regulators that shift foci dynamics and pathway choice.

Hypotheses: (1) repair foci exhibit discrete mesoscale dynamical regimes (diffuse recruitment vs coalescing droplets vs stable scaffolds) corresponding to repair pathway choice; (2) chromatin nanodomain topology constrains foci growth and coalescence; and (3) cancer-associated DDR alterations manifest as shifts in mesoscale regimes rather than complete pathway loss.

Expected insights include a cross-study atlas of foci dynamical regimes, mechanistic links between 3D genome context and emergent assembly kinetics, and open pipelines for foci tracking and integrative DDR modeling.

This requires collaboration among DDR biologists, quantitative imaging experts, proteomics analysts, and 3D genomics researchers. NCEMS support is needed to curate heterogeneous time-lapse datasets and omics, build reproducible multi-modal workflows, and train trainees in integrative analysis of mesoscale nuclear assemblies.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Patterning in Bacterial Division Machinery: A Synthesis of FtsZ Ring Architecture, Dynamics, and Cell Shape Outcomes
abstract:
Bacterial cytokinesis is driven by the FtsZ-based divisome, which forms a mesoscale ring/band (typically ~500–1000 nm circumference; ~10–50 nm filament bundles) with dynamic treadmilling. The emergent phenomenon is that collective filament organization and accessory protein patterning produce robust constriction and shape maintenance, not predictable from FtsZ polymerization alone.

We will synthesize: (i) super-resolution and cryo-ET datasets of divisome architecture across species (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR), (ii) single-molecule and time-lapse measurements of FtsZ dynamics (published tracking datasets), (iii) proteomics and interaction networks of divisome components (PRIDE; BioGRID), (iv) comparative genomics of division genes across bacteria (NCBI RefSeq), and (v) morphological phenotypes under gene perturbations and antibiotics (BacDive; published high-content imaging screens).

We will quantify ring architecture (bundle thickness, continuity, patchiness) and dynamics (treadmilling speeds, turnover) and relate these to emergent cell shape outcomes (septum symmetry, division timing, size control). Using statistical physics models of active polymers and agent-based simulations, calibrated to observed architectures, we will infer which mesoscale parameters control robustness. Comparative analysis will test how different bacteria achieve similar division outcomes with different accessory proteins.

Hypotheses: (1) divisomes operate in a constrained mesoscale regime where filament dynamics and crosslinking yield self-correcting constriction; (2) accessory proteins tune emergent ring continuity and force distribution; and (3) antibiotic susceptibilities reflect shifts in mesoscale architecture rather than direct inhibition levels.

Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of divisome mesoscale architectures, quantitative links between architecture and division robustness, and open tools for analyzing divisome imaging. This synthesis will unify structural and dynamical observations into general principles of emergent cytokinetic machinery.

Team science is required across bacterial cell biology, quantitative microscopy, biophysics, and comparative genomics. NCEMS support will enable coordinated data curation and development of reproducible pipelines and training for trainees at the interface of mesoscale structure and emergent cellular morphogenesis.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of Exosome Biogenesis Microdomains: Integrating Endosomal Proteomics, Lipidomics, and Imaging
abstract:
Exosomes originate from intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) within multivesicular bodies, formed in mesoscale endosomal microdomains (50–500 nm) enriched in ESCRT components, tetraspanins, and specific lipids. The emergent phenomenon is that collective microdomain organization yields selective cargo sorting and vesicle size distributions not predictable from individual sorting motifs.

We will synthesize: (i) exosome and endosome proteomics datasets (ExoCarta/Vesiclepedia-linked studies; PRIDE), (ii) lipidomics of extracellular vesicles and endosomal fractions (LIPID MAPS; Metabolomics Workbench), (iii) imaging datasets of ILV formation and endosomal microdomains (BioImage Archive/IDR; EMPIAR for EM of MVBs), (iv) RNA cargo profiles (exosomal RNA-seq in GEO), and (v) perturbation screens affecting EV secretion (DepMap; published CRISPR screens).

We will quantify ILV size distributions and microdomain organization from EM and fluorescence images using segmentation and spatial clustering metrics. Multi-omic integration will identify latent microdomain states defined by protein–lipid–RNA composition. Mechanistic modeling will connect ESCRT polymerization and membrane composition to observed ILV size distributions using coarse-grained membrane remodeling models. Predictive models will link microdomain states to cargo enrichment patterns.

Hypotheses: (1) exosome biogenesis proceeds through discrete mesoscale microdomain states that determine cargo classes; (2) lipid composition (ceramides, cholesterol) acts as a mesoscale controller of domain stability and ILV size; and (3) cell-type differences in EV cargo reflect microdomain state occupancy more than expression of individual cargos.

Expected insights include a unified mesoscale model of ILV microdomains, identification of compositional signatures predicting cargo selection, and open resources for EV biogenesis imaging/omics integration.

This requires team science across membrane biology, proteomics/lipidomics, quantitative imaging, and biophysical modeling. NCEMS support is needed to harmonize diverse public datasets and establish open, reproducible pipelines and training for trainees in integrative mesoscale analysis of extracellular vesicle biogenesis.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Principles of Protein Complex Stoichiometry Variability: Integrating Native MS, Cryo-EM, and Single-Cell Proteomics
abstract:
Many cellular machines exist as ensembles of stoichiometries and assembly states at mesoscale dimensions (10–100 nm complexes and supercomplexes). The emergent phenomenon is that variability in subunit stoichiometry and oligomeric state yields functional buffering and adaptability not predictable from a single “canonical” complex.

We will synthesize: (i) structures and oligomeric assemblies from PDB/EMDB, including multiple states of the same complex, (ii) native mass spectrometry and crosslinking MS datasets reporting stoichiometry distributions (PRIDE; MassIVE), (iii) single-cell and spatial proteomics measuring subunit abundance variability (Human Cell Atlas proteogenomic efforts; PRIDE single-cell proteomics), (iv) interaction networks and complex definitions (CORUM, Complex Portal), and (v) functional phenotypes from perturbation screens (DepMap) for complexes of interest (e.g., proteasome, ribosome, respiratory supercomplexes, spliceosome modules).

We will develop statistical frameworks to infer expected stoichiometry ensembles from subunit abundance distributions and binding constraints, then compare to observed ensembles from native MS and structural state catalogs. Graphical models will represent assembly pathways and predict how single-cell variability propagates to mesoscale complex heterogeneity. We will test whether certain network topologies (hub-and-spoke vs modular) produce emergent robustness by maintaining function across stoichiometry fluctuations.

Key questions: Which complexes are inherently “stoichiometrically plastic,” and what structural features enable this? Do cells exploit stoichiometry ensembles to tune function across states (stress, differentiation)? Can disease-associated perturbations be reinterpreted as shifts in ensemble distributions rather than loss of complexes?

Expected insights include a taxonomy of complex stoichiometry plasticity, predictive models linking single-cell proteomic variability to mesoscale assembly ensembles, and open tools for integrating native MS with structural and single-cell data.

This synthesis requires team science across structural biology, mass spectrometry, statistical modeling, and systems biology. NCEMS support is essential for curating heterogeneous datasets and building open, reproducible workflows and training modules for trainees to analyze emergent mesoscale behavior in protein complex ensembles.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of RNA Localization Granules in Neurons: Integrating Spatial Transcriptomics, RBP Networks, and Imaging
abstract:
Neuronal RNA localization relies on mesoscale granules and transport RNPs (50–500 nm) that package transcripts with RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and motors. The emergent phenomenon is that collective RNP assembly and composition yields selective transcript targeting and local translation programs not predictable from single zip-code motifs.

We will synthesize: (i) imaging datasets of neuronal RNA granules and transport particles (MS2/PP7, smFISH, super-resolution) from BioImage Archive/IDR, (ii) spatial transcriptomics and subcellular transcript localization datasets (e.g., APEX-seq, fractionation RNA-seq in GEO; spatial transcriptomics repositories), (iii) RBP–RNA interaction maps (eCLIP from ENCODE; POSTAR), (iv) proteomics of neuronal granules and synaptoneurosomes (PRIDE), and (v) disease-linked variants in RBPs (ClinVar; ALS/FTD gene resources).

We will build integrative models that map transcript features and RBP binding networks to mesoscale granule states. Imaging-derived granule features (size, motility classes, colocalization) will be linked to transcript localization probabilities from spatial transcriptomics. Graph neural networks will represent RBP–RNA interaction networks and predict which transcripts co-package into granules. We will test whether granules occupy discrete mesoscale compositional states corresponding to transport vs storage vs translation-ready modes.

Hypotheses: (1) selective localization emerges from mesoscale co-packaging rules driven by RBP network modularity; (2) stress and activity shift granules between states, altering local translation; and (3) neurodegenerative disease variants disrupt state transitions, increasing aberrant aggregation-like granules.

Expected insights include a cross-neuron-type atlas of granule states, predictive rules for transcript co-packaging, and open pipelines for integrating spatial transcriptomics with granule imaging.

This requires team science across neuroscience, RNA biology, quantitative imaging, and machine learning, and depends on synthesis of multiple public data modalities. NCEMS support will enable coordinated curation, open standards for granule feature reporting, and trainee training in integrative analysis of mesoscale RNP assemblies and spatial gene regulation.

title: Emergent Mesoscale Principles of Bacterial Chemoreceptor Arrays: Integrating Cryo-ET, Genomics, and Signaling Dynamics
abstract:
Bacterial chemoreceptors form large mesoscale arrays (100–500 nm patches; ~10–20 nm lattice spacing) that achieve ultrasensitive, robust chemotactic signaling. The emergent phenomenon is cooperative amplification and adaptation arising from collective lattice interactions, not predictable from single receptor properties.

We will synthesize: (i) cryo-ET datasets and subtomogram averages of chemoreceptor arrays across species (EMPIAR/EMDB), (ii) comparative genomics of chemoreceptor and signaling components (NCBI RefSeq; MiST database), (iii) biochemical and live-cell signaling dynamics datasets (FRET-based kinase activity time courses; published open data), (iv) protein structures of receptor trimers and CheA/CheW complexes (PDB/AlphaFold), and (v) ecological metadata and motility phenotypes (BacDive; literature datasets).

We will extract mesoscale lattice parameters from cryo-ET (spacing, curvature, patch size, defect density) and relate them to genomic repertoire (receptor types, adaptation enzymes) and signaling dynamics (gain, adaptation time). Using statistical mechanics models of cooperative lattices and inference methods, we will fit interaction parameters that best explain observed ultrasensitivity across species. Machine learning will predict array architecture from genomic features and environmental niche.

Hypotheses: (1) diverse bacteria converge on a limited set of lattice “operating regimes” balancing sensitivity and noise robustness; (2) lattice defects and curvature are functional, tuning dynamic range; and (3) genomic expansions of receptor repertoires correspond to predictable shifts in mesoscale array organization.

Expected insights include a comparative atlas linking array architecture to emergent signaling phenotypes and open tools for analyzing chemoreceptor tomograms. This synthesis will connect structural mesoscale organization to systems-level signaling emergence.

The project requires collaboration among cryo-ET experts, bacterial geneticists, signaling modelers, and statisticians. NCEMS support is needed to coordinate cross-species data curation and to develop open, reproducible workflows and training for trainees in integrative mesoscale structural systems biology.

title: Mesoscale Emergence of Transcription Factor Hubs: Integrating ChIP-seq, Live-Cell Imaging, and 3D Genome Data to Explain Enhancer Function
abstract:
Transcription factors (TFs) and coactivators form mesoscale hubs (50–300 nm) at enhancers, often with condensate-like properties. The emergent phenomenon is cooperative enhancer activation and specificity arising from collective hub formation, not predictable from single TF binding events.

We will synthesize: (i) ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN datasets for TFs/coactivators (ENCODE), (ii) live-cell imaging and single-molecule tracking datasets of TF clustering and residence times (IDR/BioImage Archive; published SMT datasets), (iii) 3D genome interaction data linking enhancers to promoters (HiChIP/PLAC-seq/Hi-C from 4DN/ENCODE), (iv) enhancer activity readouts (STARR-seq and MPRA datasets that are publicly available; FANTOM enhancer atlas), and (v) single-cell transcriptomics for target gene variability (Human Cell Atlas; Perturb-seq datasets in GEO).

We will infer hub features from imaging (cluster size, lifetime, mobility) and integrate them with enhancer sequence features (motif density/grammar) and 3D contact frequency. A unified model will test whether enhancer output is best predicted by a mesoscale hub variable that mediates between binding and transcription. We will use causal mediation analysis on perturbation datasets (Perturb-seq of TFs/coactivators) to distinguish direct binding effects from hub-formation effects.

Hypotheses: (1) enhancer strength and specificity are emergent properties of hub formation governed by motif grammar and cofactor availability; (2) hubs create nonlinear thresholds in transcriptional activation and noise; and (3) disease-associated noncoding variants act by disrupting hub propensity rather than eliminating binding.

Expected insights include quantitative rules linking sequence and 3D context to hub formation and emergent gene expression behavior, plus open pipelines for integrating SMT-derived clustering with genomics.

This synthesis requires team science spanning quantitative live-cell imaging, regulatory genomics, 3D genome analysis, and causal statistics. NCEMS support is essential for harmonizing heterogeneous imaging and sequencing datasets, building open reproducible workflows, and training trainees to bridge mesoscale nuclear organization with gene regulation.

title: Deciphering the Sequence Grammar of Mesoscale Viscoelasticity in Biomolecular Condensates
abstract: This project addresses the emergent phenomenon of viscoelastic transitions within biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). While the ability of proteins to phase separate is well-documented, the mesoscale material properties—such as viscosity, surface tension, and hardening over time—emerge from complex, non-linear interactions that remain poorly understood. We propose to synthesize data from the PhaSePro and DrLLPS databases, combined with structural disorder predictions from AlphaFold (pLDDT scores) and experimental rheology data scattered across literature repositories. The central hypothesis is that specific 'grammars' within intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—defined by charge patterning, residue spacing, and aromatic content—deterministically encode the emergent viscoelastic evolution of condensates, distinct from simple phase separation propensity. Our approach involves training deep learning models (specifically Graph Neural Networks) on integrated sequence-rheology datasets to map molecular features to mesoscale material states. We will validate these models by cross-referencing with cryo-electron tomography data from the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) that visualizes condensate morphology in situ. Expected insights include a predictive framework for how pathogenic aggregates (e.g., in neurodegeneration) transition from liquid to solid states, an emergent property not predictable from single-molecule dynamics. This project necessitates NCEMS support to bring together soft matter physicists, computational biologists, and machine learning experts to standardize heterogeneous rheological data and develop novel biophysical classifiers.

title: Emergent Chromatin Rheology: Synthesizing 1D Sequence and 3D Topology to Predict Nuclear Stiffness
abstract: This proposal investigates the emergent rheological properties of chromatin at the mesoscale, specifically how local genomic folding patterns dictate the physical stiffness and plasticity of the cell nucleus. The spatial organization of the genome is not merely a packing mechanism but an emergent mechanical scaffold that influences gene expression and nuclear stability. We will synthesize high-resolution Hi-C and Micro-C data from the 4D Nucleome Project, mechanics data from atomic force microscopy (AFM) studies of isolated nuclei, and transcriptomic data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). The novel hypothesis is that specific topologically associating domains (TADs) and chromatin loops act as 'mechanical springs' whose collective stiffness emerges from the interplay of epigenetic marks and loop extrusion factors, independent of the underlying DNA sequence length. By employing polymer physics simulations informed by real-world Hi-C contact maps and machine learning regression models, we aim to correlate 3D chromatin architecture with nuclear stiffness measurements. We expect to reveal how changes in mesoscale chromatin folding—driven by differentiation or disease—result in emergent mechanical softening or stiffening, impacting nuclear migration and integrity. This transdisciplinary synthesis requires a team of genomicists, mechanical engineers, and polymer physicists to bridge the gap between sequence-based genomics and physical mechanics.

title: The Emergence of Metabolic Channeling: Mapping Transient Metabolons via Integrated Interactomics
abstract: This research focuses on the emergent phenomenon of 'metabolic channeling' arising from the formation of metabolons—transient, mesoscale clusters of sequential enzymes. Unlike stable protein complexes, metabolons are dynamic structures that emerge in response to metabolic demand, creating localized pools of intermediates that increase flux and protect unstable substrates. We will synthesize protein-protein interaction (PPI) data from STRING and BioGRID, enzymatic kinetic parameters from BRENDA, and spatial proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas. Our hypothesis is that low-affinity, transient interactions between metabolic enzymes, often ignored in standard structural biology, create emergent 'super-highways' for substrates that defy diffusion-limited kinetics. The analytical strategy involves constructing spatially-constrained metabolic flux models that incorporate probability distributions of enzyme clustering derived from PPI networks. We will simulate these models to identify conditions under which channeling emerges as a dominant regulatory mechanism. Insights will likely redefine our understanding of metabolic efficiency, showing how mesoscale organization enables reaction rates impossible in a well-mixed solution. This project requires NCEMS resources to unite enzymologists, systems biologists, and network scientists to integrate static interaction maps with dynamic kinetic data.

title: Lipid Raft Dynamics and the Emergence of Signal Fidelity in T-Cell Activation
abstract: This proposal examines the emergent role of lipid rafts (mesoscale membrane nanodomains) in generating high-fidelity signaling thresholds in immune cells. T-cell receptor (TCR) triggering exhibits remarkable sensitivity and specificity, an emergent property that cannot be explained by simple ligand-receptor binding affinity. We will synthesize lipidomics datasets, single-molecule tracking data of TCR dynamics from the biological literature, and super-resolution microscopy data (STORM/PALM) available in the BioImage Archive. The central question is how the dynamic clustering of specific lipids (cholesterol, sphingolipids) and proteins creates a mesoscale 'computational engine' that filters noise and amplifies true antigenic signals. We will employ agent-based modeling and molecular dynamics simulations (coarse-grained) to integrate lipid composition data with protein mobility tracks. We expect to demonstrate that lipid rafts function as emergent signal integration hubs that undergo phase transitions to lock in activation states, providing a physical basis for immune decision-making. This synthesis requires a collaborative effort between immunologists, membrane biophysicists, and computational modelers to link compositional lipid data with spatiotemporal signaling outcomes.

title: Emergent Mechanics of the Cytoskeleton: From Molecular Motors to Cellular Tensegrity
