abstract: This project investigates how cellular stiffness and shape stability emerge from the stochastic interactions of cytoskeletal filaments and molecular motors. The mechanical integrity of a cell is an emergent property of the 'active matter' network of actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments, which behave differently than passive polymer networks. We will synthesize data from the Cytoskeleton Registry, cryo-electron tomography of cytoskeletal networks, and traction force microscopy datasets. Our hypothesis is that the cell utilizes a 'tensegrity' (tensional integrity) architecture where emergent mechanical robustness arises specifically from the interplay of compression-bearing microtubules and tension-bearing actin filaments. We will use finite element analysis (FEA) and active gel theory to model whole-cell mechanics based on the integrated structural data. The expected insight is a unified quantitative law describing how local motor activity scales up to global cell deformation and migration capabilities. This project demands a synthesis of cell biology, continuum mechanics, and computational physics, requiring NCEMS support to standardize diverse imaging and force datasets.

title: Viral Capsid Polymorphism: Emergent Geometry from Identical Subunits
abstract: This research explores the emergent phenomenon of capsid polymorphism, where identical viral coat proteins self-assemble into different mesoscale geometries (T-numbers) depending on environmental conditions. This structural plasticity is an emergent property of the subunit interaction energy landscape. We will synthesize structural data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) covering a wide range of viral families, along with thermodynamic stability data from literature. The novel question is: What are the hidden 'assembly codes' within the protein interface sequences that allow for emergent geometric flexibility versus rigidity? We will apply geometric deep learning and symmetry-aware molecular docking simulations to map the energy landscapes of capsid assembly. We expect to discover conserved interfacial motifs that act as 'hinges,' allowing emergent curvature variations that facilitate viral evolution and immune evasion. This study requires a team of structural virologists, geometric topologists, and AI researchers to analyze the vast structural space of viral assemblies.

title: The Emergence of Synaptic Memory: Nanocolumns and PSD Stability
abstract: This proposal investigates the Post-Synaptic Density (PSD) as a mesoscale storage device, where long-term synaptic plasticity emerges from the trans-synaptic alignment of 'nanocolumns' (clusters of receptors and scaffold proteins). Memory is not stored in single molecules but in the emergent stability of these supramolecular assemblies. We will synthesize super-resolution microscopy data of synaptic proteins, electrophysiological datasets (e.g., from the Allen Brain Institute), and proteomic turnover rates. Our hypothesis is that the alignment of presynaptic release sites with postsynaptic receptor nanodomains creates an emergent 'quantal efficiency' that is robust against molecular turnover. We will use reaction-diffusion simulations and stochastic modeling to integrate spatial maps with functional transmission data. Insights will reveal how the brain maintains stable information storage (memory) despite the rapid turnover of individual synaptic proteins, a fundamental paradox of neuroscience. This synthesis requires neurobiologists, biophysicists, and stochastic modelers to bridge the gap between static nanostructure and dynamic neural function.

title: Emergent Selectivity in the Nuclear Pore Complex: A Data-Driven Transport Model
abstract: This project focuses on the Nuclear Pore Complex (NPC) and the emergent phenomenon of selective transport, which arises from the disordered meshwork of FG-nucleoporins. The NPC acts as a selective gate, an emergent property that functions without energy consumption at the pore itself. We will synthesize structural models of the NPC (PDB-Dev), single-molecule transport kinetics data, and biophysical characterizations of FG-nup phase behavior. The scientific question is how the collective behavior of tethered, disordered proteins creates a 'selective filter' that allows rapid passage of transport factors while excluding inert molecules. We will employ coarse-grained molecular dynamics and polymer density functional theory to model the pore environment based on synthesized structural data. Expected insights include a unified physical model of nucleocytoplasmic transport that explains how mesoscale crowding and weak transient interactions generate emergent gating selectivity. This requires a collaboration between structural biologists, polymer physicists, and computational chemists.

title: Mitochondrial Cristae Morphodynamics and the Emergence of Bioenergetic Efficiency
abstract: This research addresses how the complex folding of mitochondrial cristae (inner membrane invaginations) leads to the emergent property of enhanced respiration efficiency and supercomplex assembly. The geometry of the cristae at the mesoscale is hypothesized to act as a proton trap, an emergent phenomenon critical for ATP synthesis. We will synthesize electron tomography data of mitochondrial ultrastructure, super-resolution imaging of respiratory chain complexes, and bioenergetic flux data. Our hypothesis is that specific cristae geometries optimize the spatial distance between proton pumps and ATP synthase, creating localized pH gradients (micro-domains) that boost efficiency beyond bulk membrane theory. We will use multiphysics simulations (combining diffusion and electrostatics) on real-world membrane geometries derived from tomography data. Insights will link mesoscale membrane architecture directly to metabolic output, relevant for understanding aging and metabolic diseases. This team science approach needs mitochondrial biologists, image analysis experts, and biophysical modelers.

title: Ribosome Collisions and the Emergence of Translational Quality Control
abstract: This proposal investigates the emergent phenomenon of 'translational bursting' and quality control arising from ribosome collisions on mRNA. While translation is often modeled as a linear process, ribosomes frequently form 'traffic jams' at the mesoscale, which serve as emergent signals for mRNA degradation or protein folding stress. We will synthesize ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) data, cryo-EM structures of colliding ribosomes, and transcriptomic decay rates. The novel hypothesis is that the spatial patterning of ribosome queues acts as a mesoscale sensor for cellular stress, integrating codon usage bias and tRNA availability into a collective decision-making process. We will develop analytical models of traffic flow on mRNA tracks to predict collision probabilities and link them to cellular outcomes found in public datasets. We expect to reveal how the cell utilizes the emergent statistics of ribosome traffic to regulate proteostasis. This requires the synthesis of genomics, structural biology, and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.

title: Emergent Synchronization in Ciliary Arrays: Hydrodynamics and Coupling
abstract: This project explores the emergent phenomenon of metachronal waves—coordinated beating patterns—in dense arrays of cilia (e.g., in the airway or brain ventricles). Individual cilia have intrinsic beat frequencies, but the macroscopic wave is an emergent property of hydrodynamic coupling. We will synthesize high-speed video microscopy data of ciliary beating, structural data of the axoneme (PDB), and fluid dynamics parameters. Our hypothesis is that emergent synchronization is robust to noise and individual defects due to long-range hydrodynamic interactions at the mesoscale. We will use computational fluid dynamics (CFD) coupled with elastic rod models to simulate ciliary fields. Insights will explain how biological systems achieve robust fluid transport and how defects in this emergent synchronization lead to ciliopathies. This necessitates a transdisciplinary team of fluid dynamicists, cell biologists, and computational physicists.

title: The Extracellular Matrix as a Mechanical Memory: Emergent Reciprocity in Tissue Homeostasis
abstract: This research investigates the emergent reciprocity between cells and the Extracellular Matrix (ECM). The ECM is not a static scaffold but a dynamic mesoscale material that accumulates 'mechanical memory' through remodeling, influencing future cell behavior. We will synthesize atomic force microscopy (AFM) maps of tissue stiffness, RNA-seq data of matrix-remodeling enzymes, and histological imaging. The central question is how local remodeling events integrate over time to create emergent stiffness gradients that guide cell migration and differentiation. We will employ agent-based models where cells modify a finite-element mesh (the ECM) based on local strain, creating a feedback loop. Expected insights include understanding how fibrosis emerges as a runaway feedback loop of this mechanical memory. This project requires NCEMS support to unite tissue engineers, data scientists, and mechanobiologists.

title: The Glycocalyx Code: Emergent Immune Evasion via Bulky Glycan Shields
abstract: This proposal examines the cell surface glycocalyx—a dense, mesoscale forest of sugars—and its emergent property of regulating immune cell access. We hypothesize that the physical height and density of the glycocalyx act as a 'kinetic trap' for immune receptors, an emergent biophysical barrier distinct from chemical recognition. We will synthesize glycomics data, atomic force microscopy measurements of cell surface height, and immune cell adhesion assays. By modeling the steric repulsion and thermodynamic entropy of the polymer brush layer using the synthesized data, we aim to predict immune evasion thresholds. Insights will reveal how cancer cells exploit this emergent physical barrier to evade T-cell attack, offering new perspectives for immunotherapy. This requires a synthesis of glycobiology, polymer physics, and immunology.

title: Symmetry Breaking in the Centrosome: Emergent Spindle Bipolarity
abstract: This project investigates the emergent phenomenon of symmetry breaking during bipolar spindle assembly. The centrosome, a mesoscale organelle, must duplicate and separate to define the axis of division. We will synthesize high-content screening image data of mitosis, phosphoproteomic time-course data, and protein interaction networks. The hypothesis is that the transition from a monopolar to a bipolar state is an emergent bifurcation driven by a threshold in motor protein forces and kinase activity gradients. We will use dynamical systems theory to model the stability landscape of spindle poles based on integrated molecular data. We expect to identify the critical control parameters that ensure robust symmetry breaking, a process that fails in cancer. This requires cell biologists, mathematicians, and image analysis experts.

title: Autophagosome Biogenesis: Emergent Membrane Remodeling from Protein Scaffolds
abstract: This research focuses on the de novo formation of the autophagosome, a mesoscale organelle that emerges from the reshaping of membrane sheets. We will synthesize data on Atg protein interactions, membrane curvature sensing, and lipid composition during starvation responses. The scientific question is how a soluble protein machinery effectively 'wets' and curls a flat membrane into a closed vesicle, an emergent topological transition. We will employ Helfrich bending energy models coupled with protein density fields derived from fluorescence microscopy data. Insights will elucidate the energetic requirements for this mesoscale remodeling and how it is regulated by cellular energy states. This synthesis needs membrane biophysicists, autophagy researchers, and computational geometers.

title: Stress Granules vs. P-Bodies: Emergent Sorting in RNA Phase Separation
abstract: This proposal investigates the emergent immiscibility and sorting of RNA between different condensate types (Stress Granules vs. P-Bodies). While both are liquid-like droplets, they maintain distinct compositions. We will synthesize RNA-seq data from isolated granules (RIP-seq), phase diagrams of RNA-binding proteins, and super-resolution imaging of granule coexistence. Our hypothesis is that the 'miscibility gap' between these organelles emerges from the competition between specific RNA-RNA base pairing and non-specific protein-RNA interactions. We will use multicomponent Flory-Huggins solution theory adapted for sequence-specific interactions to model the sorting behavior. Insights will reveal the physical rules governing how the cell compartmentalizes RNA processing without membranes. This requires RNA biologists, thermodynamicists, and data scientists.

title: Collapse of the Chaperone Network: Emergent Proteostasis Failure in Aging
abstract: This project addresses the system-level failure of protein folding, an emergent catastrophe in aging and disease. The chaperone network functions as a collective buffer, but its capacity is finite. We will synthesize proteomics data quantifying chaperone levels across age, protein aggregation datasets, and folding stability data. The novel question is: Is there a sharp 'percolation threshold' where the chaperone network suddenly loses connectivity, leading to systemic collapse? We will model the chaperone system as a flow network where capacity constraints lead to emergent congestion. We expect to define the critical tipping points of proteostasis, providing a theoretical basis for the sudden onset of age-related diseases. This requires systems biologists, network theorists, and gerontologists.

title: Emergent Antibiotic Resistance in Biofilms: The Role of Matrix Architecture
abstract: This research explores how the mesoscale architecture of the biofilm extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix confers emergent antibiotic resistance, independent of genetic mutations. We will synthesize structural data of biofilm matrices, diffusion coefficients of antibiotics through biofilms, and transcriptomic data of biofilm-dwelling bacteria. Our hypothesis is that the EPS matrix creates emergent gradients of nutrients and drugs that induce metabolic dormancy in specific spatial niches. We will use reaction-diffusion modeling on digitized biofilm architectures to predict survival rates. Insights will demonstrate how mesoscale spatial organization acts as a non-genetic mechanism of resistance. This synthesis requires microbiologists, materials scientists, and mathematical modelers.

title: GPCR Oligomerization Landscapes: Emergent Signaling Bias via Allostery
abstract: This proposal investigates G-Protein Coupled Receptor (GPCR) oligomerization (dimers/oligomers) and the resulting emergent signaling bias. GPCRs often function not as monomers but as mesoscale arrays. We will synthesize FRET/BRET data on receptor proximity, pharmacological response data, and molecular dynamics simulations of receptor interfaces. The central question is how the geometry of the oligomer alters the allosteric pathway of the receptor, creating emergent signaling profiles (e.g., G-protein vs. Arrestin bias) not seen in monomers. We will use statistical thermodynamic models to link oligomer populations to signaling outputs. Insights will guide the design of drugs that target specific oligomeric states, requiring pharmacologists, structural biologists, and computational chemists.

title: Nuclear Speckles as Splicing Hubs: Emergent Amplification of Gene Expression
abstract: This project examines Nuclear Speckles as mesoscale reaction crucibles that enhance splicing efficiency. We will synthesize spatial transcriptomics data, splicing efficiency metrics (intron retention rates), and imaging of speckle proximity. The hypothesis is that the high local concentration of splicing factors in speckles creates an emergent 'kinetic boost' for specific subsets of genes, regulated by their distance to the speckle. We will correlate 3D genomic distance to speckles with splicing kinetics using integrated datasets. Insights will reveal a spatial code of gene regulation where nuclear position determines processing efficiency. This requires genomicists, cell biologists, and spatial statisticians.

title: Thylakoid Stacking and the Emergence of Photosynthetic Robustness
abstract: This research investigates the mesoscale stacking of plant thylakoid membranes (grana) and the emergent property of light harvesting robustness. We will synthesize cryo-ET data of thylakoid architecture, spectroscopic data on energy transfer, and environmental stress response data. The question is how the dynamic stacking/unstacking of membranes regulates energy distribution between Photosystem I and II, an emergent mechanism to prevent photodamage. We will use excitonic energy transfer models on realistic membrane geometries. Insights will explain how plants manage fluctuating light environments through mesoscale structural remodeling. This requires plant biologists, quantum biologists, and structural modelers.

title: Exosome Loading and Sorting: Emergent Communication Packets
abstract: This proposal focuses on the selective loading of cargo into exosomes, creating mesoscale vectors for intercellular communication. We will synthesize vesicle content databases (ExoCarta), protein-lipid interaction data, and biogenesis pathway data. The hypothesis is that cargo sorting is an emergent property of membrane curvature sensing and microdomain partitioning at the budding site. We will model the sorting thermodynamics to predict cargo enrichment based on molecular properties. Insights will reveal the 'addressing system' of extracellular vesicles, crucial for understanding their role in metastasis and therapy. This requires vesicle biologists, biophysicists, and data scientists.

title: Synthetic Cell Assembly: Predicting Emergent Life-like Behaviors from Component Integration
abstract: This final project proposes a meta-synthesis of data from 'bottom-up' synthetic biology to understand the minimal requirements for emergent life-like behaviors (motility, division, homeostasis). We will synthesize data from disparate synthetic cell projects (e.g., liposome encapsulation, minimal genome reconstitution). The goal is to train machine learning models to predict which combinations of modules (energy, information, containment) yield emergent system-level stability vs. collapse. This is the ultimate test of understanding emergence: can we predict the transition from non-living matter to a living system? This requires a broad coalition of synthetic biologists, systems theorists, and AI researchers to define the design rules of life at the mesoscale.

title: Emergent Phase Separation Grammar: Decoding How Intrinsically Disordered Region Sequence Patterns Drive Mesoscale Condensate Properties
abstract: Biomolecular condensates represent a paradigmatic example of mesoscale emergence, where intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) self-organize into membraneless organelles with properties not predictable from individual molecular components. This synthesis project will decode the 'grammar' connecting IDP sequence features to emergent condensate behaviors by integrating multiple public datasets. We will synthesize structural data from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), disorder predictions from MobiDB and DisProt, phase separation propensity scores from PhaSePro and LLPSDB, proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas, and single-cell RNA-seq data from the Human Cell Atlas to understand how sequence-encoded information translates to mesoscale organization. The central hypothesis is that specific combinations of sequence motifs—rather than individual features—create emergent interaction networks that dictate condensate material properties, composition, and cellular function. We will employ natural language processing approaches adapted for protein sequences, treating amino acid patterns as a 'language' with grammatical rules governing phase behavior. Machine learning models will identify synergistic motif combinations that predict condensate viscosity, surface tension, and client recruitment capacity. Network analysis will map how these sequence features create emergent interaction topologies at the mesoscale. Graph neural networks will model the collective behavior of multiple IDP chains, predicting how molecular-level interactions scale to condensate-level properties. A key innovation is correlating sequence grammar with cellular phenotypes by integrating GWAS data from the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog, connecting IDP variants to disease states through altered mesoscale organization. This project requires transdisciplinary collaboration between computational biophysicists expert in IDP behavior, machine learning specialists in sequence analysis, cell biologists studying condensate function, and statistical geneticists linking variants to phenotypes. The synthesis spans molecular sequence databases, structural repositories, cellular imaging archives, and population genetics resources—a scope impossible for any single laboratory. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework for condensate properties from sequence, identification of 'grammatical rules' governing phase separation, and mechanistic insights into how condensate dysregulation causes disease. All analysis pipelines, trained models, and curated datasets will be publicly released following FAIR principles. This work will transform our understanding of how information encoded in linear sequences emerges as three-dimensional mesoscale organization with distinct functional properties.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Ribosome Clustering: Synthesizing Cryo-ET and Ribosome Profiling Data to Understand Emergent Translation Factories
abstract: Translation occurs not through isolated ribosomes but within dynamic mesoscale clusters called 'translation factories' or polysomes, where emergent properties arise from ribosome cooperation. This synthesis project investigates how ribosome clustering creates emergent translational behaviors—including enhanced processivity, coordinated protein folding, and localized mRNA regulation—that cannot be predicted from single ribosome properties. We will integrate cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) data from EMPIAR and EMDB revealing in-situ ribosome spatial organization, ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) data from GEO and GWIPS-viz capturing translation dynamics, structural data from PDB on ribosome-associated factors, and proteomics from PRIDE quantifying translation machinery stoichiometry. The central question is: how do spatial arrangements of ribosomes at the mesoscale (50-500 nm polysome structures) create emergent translational properties distinct from summed individual ribosome activities? Our computational approach combines spatial statistics analysis of cryo-ET reconstructions to characterize ribosome clustering patterns, kinetic modeling of translation dynamics informed by Ribo-seq pausing patterns, and agent-based simulations of polysome behavior. We will develop novel algorithms to segment and classify polysome architectures from tomographic data, then correlate these structures with mRNA-specific translation efficiencies from Ribo-seq. Machine learning will identify features of polysome organization predictive of translation output, protein folding efficiency, and co-translational assembly. Integration with protein-protein interaction networks from STRING and BioGRID will reveal how nascent chain interactions within polysomes enable emergent co-translational complex assembly. This project demands expertise spanning cryo-ET image analysis, translation biology, mathematical modeling, and machine learning—capabilities distributed across specialized laboratories. The data synthesis challenge involves reconciling structural snapshots with dynamic sequencing readouts across different experimental systems. Expected insights include principles governing polysome architecture, quantitative relationships between mesoscale ribosome organization and translation output, and mechanisms of emergent co-translational protein folding. Deliverables include open-source tools for polysome analysis, curated cross-referenced datasets, and predictive models of translation factory behavior. Understanding these emergent translation properties has implications for synthetic biology and diseases involving translation dysregulation.

title: Emergent Mechanics of the Nuclear Pore Complex: Integrating Structural, Biophysical, and Transport Data to Model Collective Gating Behavior
abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) exemplifies mesoscale emergence: ~500 intrinsically disordered FG-nucleoporins create a selective barrier with transport properties unpredictable from individual protein behaviors. This synthesis project will develop comprehensive models of emergent NPC gating by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB capturing NPC architecture, molecular dynamics trajectories from GPCRmd and similar repositories, single-molecule transport kinetics from published studies compiled in curated databases, FG-nup sequence data from UniProt, and nuclear proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas defining cargo flux. The fundamental question is: how do collective FG-nup dynamics create the emergent selective barrier that simultaneously enables rapid transport of specific cargoes while excluding others? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from mesoscale FG-nup network properties—including collective conformational states, transient crosslinks, and cargo-induced reorganization—rather than simple additive binding interactions. Our analytical approach employs coarse-grained molecular dynamics informed by structural data to simulate FG-nup meshwork behavior, network theory to model connectivity patterns, and machine learning to identify collective states from simulation ensembles. We will develop Markov state models capturing transitions between emergent barrier configurations, correlating these with experimental transport rates. Integration of phosphoproteomics data from PhosphoSitePlus will reveal how post-translational modifications tune emergent barrier properties. Cross-species comparative analysis using orthologous NPC data will identify conserved principles of emergent selectivity. This project requires collaboration between structural biologists interpreting NPC architecture, polymer physicists modeling FG-nup behavior, computational chemists running simulations, and cell biologists understanding transport regulation. The synthesis challenge—connecting angstrom-scale structural data to nanometer-scale meshwork organization to micron-scale transport phenotypes—exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models of emergent NPC selectivity, identification of collective FG-nup states governing transport, and principles applicable to designing synthetic selective barriers. All simulation protocols, analysis code, and model parameters will be openly shared, enabling community refinement of NPC models.

title: Chromatin Compartmentalization Dynamics: Synthesizing Hi-C, Imaging, and Epigenomic Data to Model Emergent Nuclear Organization
abstract: Chromatin organization into A/B compartments, topologically associating domains (TADs), and nuclear bodies represents emergent mesoscale structure arising from DNA-protein interactions. This synthesis project will integrate multi-modal data to understand how molecular-level chromatin modifications create emergent nuclear compartmentalization with functional consequences. We will synthesize Hi-C contact maps from 4DN Data Portal and ENCODE, super-resolution imaging data from the Image Data Resource and Cell Image Library, ChIP-seq for histone modifications and chromatin proteins from ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics, ATAC-seq accessibility data, and single-cell multi-omics from the Human Cell Atlas. The central hypothesis is that emergent compartmentalization arises from phase separation driven by multivalent interactions among modified histones and reader proteins, creating mesoscale domains (100 nm - 1 μm) with distinct biochemical environments. We will develop integrative computational frameworks combining polymer physics models of chromatin, machine learning for predicting 3D organization from sequence and epigenetic features, and spatial statistics for analyzing imaging data. Novel algorithms will integrate contact frequencies with spatial positions, resolving the relationship between measured interactions and physical distances. Network analysis will identify emergent chromatin communities and their hierarchical organization. We will correlate compartmentalization patterns with transcriptional output using RNA-seq from matched samples, testing whether emergent nuclear organization causally influences gene expression or vice versa. Cross-cell-type analysis will reveal conserved versus cell-specific emergent organizational principles. This project demands expertise in chromosome biology, polymer physics, image analysis, machine learning, and genomics—requiring collaboration across traditionally separate fields. The data integration challenge spans contact maps, images, and sequencing data at different resolutions and from different experimental systems. Expected insights include quantitative models of compartmentalization emergence, identification of key molecular drivers of mesoscale organization, and understanding of how nuclear structure influences function. All analysis pipelines, trained models, and integrated datasets will be publicly released, establishing resources for the chromosome biology community.

title: Emergent Allostery in Protein Complexes: Mining Structural Databases to Discover Long-Range Communication Networks
abstract: Allosteric regulation in multi-subunit protein complexes represents emergent behavior where binding events at one site influence distant sites through collective conformational changes—properties absent in isolated subunits. This synthesis project will systematically discover and characterize emergent allosteric networks by mining structural databases. We will integrate the Protein Data Bank (>200,000 structures), molecular dynamics trajectories from MDAnalysis and related repositories, hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) data from HDXsite, and mutational fitness landscapes from deep mutational scanning datasets in MaveDB. The central question is: what structural and dynamic features enable emergent long-range communication in protein complexes that individual subunits lack? We hypothesize that emergent allostery requires specific mesoscale organizational features—interface geometries, dynamic coupling patterns, and evolutionary constraints—that create communication pathways spanning 10-100 nm distances. Our computational approach combines graph-theoretical analysis of structure networks, normal mode analysis for collective motions, machine learning to predict allosteric sites from structural features, and evolutionary analysis to identify co-evolving residue networks. We will develop algorithms to automatically identify allosteric pathways by analyzing conformational ensembles across ligand-bound and apo states. Integration with disease mutation databases (ClinVar, COSMIC) will connect disrupted allosteric networks to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across protein families will reveal conserved principles of emergent allostery versus family-specific mechanisms. This project requires expertise spanning structural biology, protein dynamics, evolutionary biology, and machine learning—necessitating collaboration between computationally-focused and experimentally-informed laboratories. The synthesis of structural, dynamic, evolutionary, and phenotypic data across thousands of protein complexes exceeds any single lab's capacity. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive atlas of emergent allosteric networks, predictive models for allosteric site identification, and mechanistic principles governing long-range communication. All databases, analysis tools, and predictive models will be openly released, enabling rational design of allosteric modulators and understanding of how complex-level properties emerge from subunit assembly.

title: Cytoskeletal Crosstalk at the Mesoscale: Integrating Structural and Live-Cell Data to Model Emergent Mechanical Properties
abstract: The cytoskeleton exhibits emergent mechanical properties arising from interactions among actin filaments, microtubules, and intermediate filaments at the mesoscale. This synthesis project will decode how cytoskeletal crosstalk creates emergent cellular mechanics by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize cryo-ET data from EMPIAR showing cytoskeletal architecture, super-resolution microscopy from the Image Data Resource, mechanical measurements from published atomic force microscopy and optical trap studies, proteomics of cytoskeletal interactomes from BioPlex and hu.MAP, and transcriptomics correlating cytoskeletal gene expression with mechanical phenotypes. The fundamental question is: how do interactions between different cytoskeletal systems at the mesoscale (100 nm - 10 μm) create emergent mechanical properties—stiffness, viscosity, active stress generation—that individual filament types cannot produce? We hypothesize that crosslinker proteins create emergent mechanical coupling by forming dynamic networks whose properties depend on mesoscale organization rather than simple component addition. Our analytical approach combines finite element modeling of cytoskeletal networks informed by structural data, agent-based simulations of crosslinker dynamics, and machine learning to predict mechanical properties from network topology. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cytoskeletal organization from diverse imaging modalities, creating standardized descriptors of mesoscale architecture. Network analysis will identify key nodes (crosslinkers, motors) whose perturbation maximally alters emergent mechanics. Integration with cell migration and morphogenesis datasets will connect mesoscale cytoskeletal organization to cellular behaviors. This project demands expertise in cytoskeletal biology, mechanical engineering, image analysis, and computational modeling—capabilities distributed across different research communities. The synthesis challenge involves reconciling structural data, mechanical measurements, and cellular phenotypes across experimental systems. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent cytoskeletal mechanics, identification of key crosslinkers governing mechanical coupling, and principles for engineering cellular mechanical properties. All analysis tools, simulation code, and curated datasets will be openly shared, advancing both fundamental understanding and mechanobiology applications.

title: Emergent Specificity in Kinase-Substrate Networks: Synthesizing Phosphoproteomics and Structural Data to Decode Signaling Fidelity
abstract: Cellular signaling networks achieve remarkable specificity despite kinases sharing similar catalytic mechanisms—an emergent property arising from mesoscale organization including scaffolds, localization, and temporal dynamics. This synthesis project will decode how emergent specificity arises by integrating phosphoproteomics, structural biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize phosphoproteomic data from PhosphoSitePlus and PRIDE (>300,000 phosphosites), kinase-substrate relationships from PhosphoSitePlus and KinaseNET, structural data from PDB on kinase-substrate complexes, protein localization from the Human Protein Atlas, and protein-protein interactions from BioGRID and STRING. The central hypothesis is that signaling specificity emerges from mesoscale organizational features—scaffold-mediated co-localization, compartmentalization, and kinetic proofreading networks—rather than intrinsic kinase-substrate affinity alone. We will develop computational frameworks integrating sequence-based kinase specificity predictions with spatial and temporal context. Machine learning models will predict phosphorylation events by combining kinase motif recognition with localization overlap, scaffold interactions, and network topology. We will construct dynamic models of signaling cascades incorporating mesoscale organization, testing whether emergent specificity requires spatial constraints. Analysis of phosphoproteomic time-series data will reveal how temporal ordering creates emergent pathway specificity. Integration with disease mutation data from COSMIC and ClinVar will identify how disrupted mesoscale organization causes aberrant signaling. Cross-species comparative analysis will distinguish conserved emergent specificity mechanisms from species-specific adaptations. This project requires collaboration between signaling biologists, structural biologists, computational modelers, and data scientists—expertise distributed across institutions. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, localization, and interaction data at proteome scale exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent signaling specificity, identification of key organizational features enabling fidelity, and principles for predicting signaling outcomes. All predictive models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released, enabling rational intervention in signaling pathways.

title: Metabolon Assembly and Emergent Metabolic Channeling: Integrating Structural, Metabolomic, and Interactome Data
abstract: Metabolons—transient enzyme assemblies enabling substrate channeling—represent emergent mesoscale organization where metabolic efficiency exceeds predictions from isolated enzyme kinetics. This synthesis project will systematically characterize metabolon organization and emergent channeling by integrating diverse public datasets. We will synthesize protein-protein interaction data from BioGRID and IntAct, structural data from PDB on enzyme complexes, metabolomics from MetaboLights and the Human Metabolome Database, enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, and proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas. The fundamental question is: how does mesoscale enzyme clustering create emergent metabolic properties—enhanced flux, reduced intermediate accumulation, pathway insulation—that isolated enzymes cannot achieve? We hypothesize that metabolon assembly creates microenvironments with emergent kinetic properties determined by enzyme stoichiometry, spatial arrangement, and dynamic association/dissociation. Our computational approach combines constraint-based metabolic modeling incorporating channeling, molecular docking to predict enzyme complex geometries, and kinetic simulations of substrate transfer within assemblies. We will develop algorithms to identify putative metabolons from interaction networks, validating predictions against metabolomic signatures of channeling (reduced free intermediate pools). Machine learning will predict metabolon formation propensity from enzyme properties and cellular conditions. Integration with transcriptomic data will reveal how metabolon assembly responds to metabolic demands. Analysis across organisms will identify conserved metabolon architectures versus species-specific adaptations. This project demands expertise in metabolism, structural biology, systems biology, and computational chemistry—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of interaction, structural, kinetic, and metabolomic data across metabolic pathways exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive metabolon atlas, predictive models of emergent channeling efficiency, and principles governing metabolon assembly. Understanding emergent metabolic organization has implications for metabolic engineering and diseases involving metabolic dysfunction. All databases, models, and analysis tools will be openly released following FAIR principles.

title: Emergent Selectivity of Autophagy Receptors: Synthesizing Structural and Proteomic Data to Decode Cargo Recognition Networks
abstract: Selective autophagy achieves remarkable cargo specificity through receptor proteins that bridge substrates to autophagosomes—an emergent property arising from multivalent interactions at the mesoscale. This synthesis project will decode how autophagy receptors create emergent selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on receptor-cargo and receptor-LC3 complexes, autophagy interactomes from BioGRID and published studies, ubiquitin-modified proteomics from PhosphoSitePlus, organelle proteomics from the Human Protein Atlas, and autophagy flux measurements from published screens. The central question is: how do autophagy receptors create emergent selectivity at the mesoscale (10-1000 nm cargo structures) through avidity effects, coincidence detection, and cooperative binding that individual receptor-cargo interactions cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from receptor oligomerization, multivalent cargo recognition, and phase separation creating receptor condensates that amplify weak individual interactions. Our computational approach combines structural modeling of receptor-cargo assemblies, network analysis of autophagy interactomes, and machine learning to predict cargo selectivity from receptor and cargo features. We will develop coarse-grained simulations of receptor clustering on cargo surfaces, testing how avidity emerges from receptor density and cargo geometry. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted receptor-cargo recognition to pathological cargo accumulation. Comparative analysis across selective autophagy pathways (mitophagy, aggrephagy, xenophagy) will reveal shared versus pathway-specific emergent selectivity mechanisms. This project requires expertise in autophagy biology, structural biology, computational modeling, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and phenotypic data across autophagy pathways exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models of emergent selectivity, identification of key features determining cargo recognition, and principles for engineering selective autophagy. All analysis tools, models, and curated datasets will be openly released, advancing understanding of this therapeutically important pathway.

title: Emergent Timing in Circadian Protein Networks: Integrating Structural Dynamics with Systems-Level Oscillations
abstract: Circadian rhythms emerge from protein interaction networks where no individual component oscillates—a striking example of mesoscale emergence where system-level timing properties arise from molecular interactions. This synthesis project will decode how circadian timing emerges by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and systems biology datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on clock protein complexes, phosphoproteomics time-series from published circadian studies, protein-protein interactions from BioGRID, transcriptomics from CircaDB and CGDB, and protein stability measurements from published datasets. The fundamental question is: how do post-translational modifications and protein-protein interactions at the mesoscale create emergent oscillatory behavior with ~24-hour periodicity? We hypothesize that emergent timing arises from coupled feedback loops operating through mesoscale protein complexes whose assembly/disassembly dynamics create delays essential for oscillation. Our computational approach combines mathematical modeling of circadian networks, molecular dynamics simulations of clock protein complexes, and machine learning to identify structural features governing interaction kinetics. We will develop models incorporating explicit protein complex formation, testing how mesoscale assembly creates emergent delays. Analysis of phosphoproteomic time-series will reveal how modification cascades propagate through clock protein networks. Integration with tissue-specific expression data will explain how the same molecular components generate different emergent periods across tissues. Comparative analysis across species will identify conserved emergent timing mechanisms versus species-specific adaptations. This project demands expertise in circadian biology, structural biology, mathematical modeling, and proteomics—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of structural, dynamic, and systems-level data across circadian networks exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include mechanistic models connecting molecular interactions to emergent periodicity, identification of key mesoscale organizational features determining timing, and principles for modulating circadian rhythms. Understanding emergent circadian timing has implications for chronotherapy and metabolic diseases. All models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Proton Gradients in Mitochondrial Cristae: Synthesizing Cryo-ET and Bioenergetic Data to Model Mesoscale Energy Transduction
abstract: Mitochondrial cristae architecture creates emergent proton gradients that enhance ATP synthesis efficiency beyond predictions from flat membrane models—a mesoscale phenomenon coupling structure to function. This synthesis project will decode how cristae geometry creates emergent bioenergetic properties by integrating structural and functional datasets. We will synthesize cryo-ET data from EMPIAR showing cristae ultrastructure, respiratory chain complex structures from PDB, proteomics of mitochondrial composition from MitoCarta and IMPI, metabolomics from MetaboLights, and bioenergetic measurements from published studies. The central question is: how does cristae morphology at the mesoscale (50-500 nm invaginations) create emergent proton concentration gradients and ATP synthesis rates that flat membranes cannot achieve? We hypothesize that cristae geometry creates microcompartments where local proton concentrations exceed bulk predictions, and that respiratory chain supercomplex organization within cristae optimizes proton delivery to ATP synthase. Our computational approach combines finite element modeling of proton diffusion within cristae geometries extracted from tomograms, molecular simulations of supercomplex organization, and systems biology modeling of oxidative phosphorylation incorporating spatial structure. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cristae morphology across cell types and conditions, correlating architecture with bioenergetic output. Integration with disease mutation data will connect cristae morphology defects to mitochondrial dysfunction. Comparative analysis across species and tissues will reveal how emergent bioenergetic optimization adapts to metabolic demands. This project requires expertise in mitochondrial biology, cryo-ET, biophysical modeling, and systems biology—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and bioenergetic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent proton gradients, identification of key architectural features optimizing ATP synthesis, and principles governing cristae-bioenergetics relationships. Understanding emergent mitochondrial function has implications for aging and metabolic diseases. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Antigen Processing in the Immunoproteasome: Integrating Structural and Immunopeptidomic Data to Model Epitope Generation
abstract: The immunoproteasome generates MHC-presented peptides through emergent cleavage patterns that differ from constitutive proteasomes—a mesoscale phenomenon where subunit composition alters processing outcomes. This synthesis project will decode how immunoproteasome assembly creates emergent epitope generation by integrating structural biology and immunopeptidomics. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of proteasome variants, immunopeptidomic data from IEDB and SysteMHC Atlas, protein sequence data from UniProt, and transcriptomics correlating proteasome subunit expression with peptide repertoires. The central question is: how does immunoproteasome subunit incorporation create emergent cleavage specificities at the mesoscale (the ~15 nm proteasome barrel) that individual catalytic subunits cannot produce? We hypothesize that emergent cleavage patterns arise from allosteric communication between subunits, altered substrate threading, and cooperative effects among catalytic sites that depend on mesoscale proteasome architecture. Our computational approach combines structural modeling of substrate processing through proteasome channels, machine learning to predict cleavage sites from sequence and proteasome composition, and network analysis of epitope generation pathways. We will develop algorithms correlating proteasome subunit expression patterns with immunopeptidome composition across cell types. Integration with T cell epitope databases will connect emergent cleavage to immune recognition. Analysis across disease states (cancer, infection, autoimmunity) will reveal how altered proteasome composition shifts emergent epitope generation. This project demands expertise in proteasome biology, immunology, structural biology, and machine learning—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of structural, immunopeptidomic, and expression data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent epitope generation, identification of key subunit interactions governing cleavage specificity, and principles for modulating antigen processing. Understanding emergent immunoproteasome function has implications for vaccine design and cancer immunotherapy. All predictive models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Selectivity in Nuclear Export: Synthesizing Structural and Transport Data to Model CRM1-Mediated Cargo Recognition
abstract: CRM1-mediated nuclear export achieves selective transport of hundreds of cargoes through a single receptor—emergent selectivity arising from mesoscale complex assembly rather than simple binary interactions. This synthesis project will decode emergent export selectivity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and transport kinetics. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on CRM1-cargo complexes, nuclear export signal (NES) sequences from NESdb and ValidNES, proteomics of nuclear/cytoplasmic distribution from the Human Protein Atlas, and transport kinetics from published single-molecule studies. The central question is: how does CRM1 achieve emergent selectivity for diverse cargoes through mesoscale ternary complex formation with RanGTP that binary CRM1-cargo interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent selectivity arises from conformational selection, where RanGTP binding creates allosteric changes in CRM1 that differentially stabilize cargo complexes based on NES properties beyond simple affinity. Our computational approach combines molecular dynamics simulations of CRM1-RanGTP-cargo assemblies, machine learning to predict export efficiency from NES sequence and structure, and kinetic modeling of transport incorporating complex assembly dynamics. We will develop algorithms correlating NES features with export kinetics, identifying sequence and structural determinants of emergent selectivity. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted export to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across CRM1 cargoes will reveal shared versus cargo-specific emergent recognition mechanisms. This project requires expertise in nuclear transport, structural biology, computational chemistry, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, sequence, localization, and kinetic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent export selectivity, identification of key features determining cargo recognition, and principles for modulating nuclear export. Understanding emergent transport selectivity has implications for diseases involving mislocalized proteins. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Cooperativity in Transcription Factor Clusters: Synthesizing ChIP-seq, Structural, and Imaging Data to Model Enhancer Activation
abstract: Transcription factor (TF) clustering at enhancers creates emergent transcriptional outputs through cooperative DNA binding and co-activator recruitment—mesoscale phenomena where clustered TFs achieve regulatory outcomes impossible for isolated factors. This synthesis project will decode emergent TF cooperativity by integrating genomics, structural biology, and imaging datasets. We will synthesize ChIP-seq data from ENCODE and ReMap, structural data from PDB on TF-DNA complexes, super-resolution imaging of TF clusters from published studies, and transcriptomics correlating TF binding with gene expression. The central question is: how does TF clustering at enhancers (mesoscale assemblies of 10-100 TF molecules) create emergent transcriptional activation that isolated TF binding cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent cooperativity arises from multivalent interactions among TF activation domains, DNA-mediated TF-TF communication, and phase separation creating transcriptional condensates. Our computational approach combines thermodynamic modeling of cooperative DNA binding, machine learning to predict enhancer activity from TF binding patterns, and spatial simulations of TF clustering dynamics. We will develop algorithms integrating ChIP-seq occupancy with structural constraints on TF spacing, predicting cooperative binding configurations. Analysis of single-cell transcriptomics will connect TF cluster heterogeneity to transcriptional noise. Integration with GWAS data will link variants affecting emergent cooperativity to disease phenotypes. This project demands expertise in transcriptional regulation, structural biology, imaging analysis, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of genomic, structural, and imaging data across regulatory elements exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent TF cooperativity, identification of key features enabling enhancer activation, and principles for predicting transcriptional output from TF binding. Understanding emergent transcriptional regulation has implications for gene therapy and developmental biology. All models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Viral Assembly: Synthesizing Cryo-EM and Sequence Data to Model How Capsid Geometry Arises from Protein Interactions
abstract: Viral capsid assembly exemplifies emergent mesoscale organization where hundreds of protein subunits self-organize into precise icosahedral structures with properties unpredictable from individual proteins. This synthesis project will decode emergent capsid assembly by integrating structural biology, biophysics, and evolutionary data. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB across viral families, capsid protein sequences from UniProt and NCBI, assembly kinetics from published studies, and evolutionary data on capsid diversification. The central question is: how do local protein-protein interactions create emergent global capsid geometry at the mesoscale (20-200 nm particles) with precise curvature, symmetry, and stability? We hypothesize that emergent geometry arises from conformational switching at quasi-equivalent positions, where identical proteins adopt different local environments to achieve global curvature—a mesoscale organizational principle. Our computational approach combines coarse-grained molecular dynamics of capsid assembly, graph-theoretical analysis of protein interaction networks in capsids, and machine learning to predict assembly outcomes from protein sequences. We will develop algorithms to extract interaction rules from structural data, testing whether minimal rule sets can recapitulate emergent capsid geometries. Evolutionary analysis will reveal how emergent assembly properties constrain capsid protein evolution. Integration with fitness data from deep mutational scanning will connect assembly defects to viral phenotypes. This project requires expertise in virology, structural biology, polymer physics, and evolutionary biology—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, sequence, kinetic, and evolutionary data across viral families exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include general principles of emergent capsid assembly, predictive models of assembly from sequence, and understanding of how evolution shapes emergent viral architecture. Understanding emergent viral assembly has implications for antiviral design and nanotechnology. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Membrane Curvature Sensing: Integrating Structural and Lipidomic Data to Model BAR Domain Collective Behavior
abstract: BAR domain proteins sense and generate membrane curvature through emergent collective behavior at the mesoscale—properties arising from oligomerization and membrane remodeling that individual proteins cannot achieve. This synthesis project will decode emergent curvature sensing by integrating structural biology, lipidomics, and biophysics datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on BAR domain proteins, lipidomic data from LIPID MAPS and LipidBank, membrane curvature measurements from published studies, and proteomics of membrane-associated proteins from the Human Protein Atlas. The central question is: how do BAR domain proteins create emergent curvature sensitivity and membrane remodeling at the mesoscale (10-100 nm membrane deformations) through collective assembly? We hypothesize that emergent curvature sensing arises from cooperative BAR domain oligomerization on curved membranes, creating positive feedback between protein binding and curvature generation. Our computational approach combines coarse-grained molecular dynamics of BAR domains on membranes, continuum mechanical modeling of membrane deformation, and machine learning to predict curvature preferences from BAR domain structure. We will develop algorithms correlating BAR domain structural features with curvature sensing and generation capabilities. Integration with cellular imaging data will connect in vitro emergent behavior to in vivo membrane remodeling. Analysis across BAR domain families will reveal conserved versus specialized emergent properties. This project demands expertise in membrane biology, structural biology, biophysics, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of structural, lipidomic, and biophysical data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent curvature sensing, identification of key features determining BAR domain function, and principles for engineering membrane-remodeling proteins. Understanding emergent membrane remodeling has implications for endocytosis, cell division, and neurological diseases. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Prion Strain Properties: Synthesizing Cryo-EM Structures with Clinical Data to Model How Fibril Architecture Determines Pathology
abstract: Prion strains exhibit emergent pathological properties—distinct incubation periods, tissue tropisms, and clinical presentations—arising from mesoscale fibril architectures rather than sequence differences. This synthesis project will decode how fibril structure creates emergent strain properties by integrating structural biology, neuropathology, and clinical datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of prion and prion-like fibrils, clinical data from published prion disease cohorts, neuropathological descriptions from brain bank studies, and sequence data from UniProt. The central question is: how does fibril architecture at the mesoscale (fibril cross-sections of ~10 nm, lengths of 100-1000 nm) create emergent strain-specific pathological properties? We hypothesize that emergent strain properties arise from fibril surface features, fragmentation propensities, and cellular interaction interfaces determined by core architecture. Our computational approach combines structural analysis of fibril polymorphs, machine learning to correlate architectural features with clinical phenotypes, and kinetic modeling of fibril propagation and fragmentation. We will develop algorithms to quantify fibril structural features predictive of strain behavior. Integration with cellular toxicity data will connect fibril properties to emergent pathological mechanisms. Comparative analysis across prion-like proteins (α-synuclein, tau, Aβ) will reveal shared principles of emergent strain determination. This project requires expertise in prion biology, structural biology, neuropathology, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, clinical, and pathological data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include models connecting fibril architecture to emergent pathology, identification of key structural features determining strain properties, and principles for predicting disease outcomes from fibril structure. Understanding emergent prion strain properties has implications for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis and therapy. All analysis pipelines, models, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Cell Polarity from Protein Localization Networks: Synthesizing Imaging and Interactome Data to Model Symmetry Breaking
abstract: Cell polarity emerges from protein localization networks where initially uniform distributions spontaneously break symmetry—a mesoscale phenomenon where spatial organization arises from molecular interactions. This synthesis project will decode emergent polarity by integrating imaging, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize protein localization data from the Human Protein Atlas and Cell Image Library, protein-protein interactions from BioGRID, phosphoproteomics from PhosphoSitePlus, and live-cell imaging from published studies capturing polarity establishment. The central question is: how do reaction-diffusion networks of polarity proteins create emergent spatial organization at the mesoscale (1-10 μm polarity domains) from initially homogeneous distributions? We hypothesize that emergent polarity arises from positive feedback loops in membrane-cytoplasm cycling, mutual antagonism between polarity complexes, and scaffolding interactions that amplify initial asymmetries. Our computational approach combines reaction-diffusion modeling of polarity networks, machine learning to predict polarity outcomes from protein expression patterns, and image analysis to quantify polarity establishment dynamics. We will develop algorithms integrating interaction networks with spatial localization data, testing which network motifs are necessary and sufficient for emergent symmetry breaking. Integration with single-cell RNA-seq will connect polarity protein expression heterogeneity to polarity establishment variability. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal conserved versus specialized emergent polarity mechanisms. This project demands expertise in cell polarity, mathematical modeling, image analysis, and systems biology—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of imaging, interaction, and expression data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent polarity, identification of minimal network requirements for symmetry breaking, and principles for engineering polarized cells. Understanding emergent polarity has implications for development, cancer, and tissue engineering. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Specificity in Ubiquitin Chain Recognition: Synthesizing Structural and Proteomic Data to Decode the Ubiquitin Code
abstract: The 'ubiquitin code'—where different polyubiquitin chain types specify distinct cellular outcomes—represents emergent signaling specificity arising from mesoscale chain conformations rather than simple ubiquitin-receptor binding. This synthesis project will decode emergent chain specificity by integrating structural biology, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize structural data from PDB on ubiquitin chains and receptor complexes, ubiquitin-modified proteomics from PhosphoSitePlus and published studies, ubiquitin receptor interactomes from BioGRID, and functional data from published screens. The central question is: how do polyubiquitin chain conformations at the mesoscale (chains of 2-10 ubiquitins spanning 5-50 nm) create emergent signaling specificity that monoubiquitin cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent specificity arises from chain-type-specific conformational ensembles that present distinct binding surfaces, enabling avidity-based discrimination by multivalent receptors. Our computational approach combines molecular dynamics simulations of polyubiquitin chains, machine learning to predict chain-receptor binding from structural features, and network analysis of ubiquitin signaling pathways. We will develop algorithms correlating chain conformational properties with receptor selectivity. Integration with disease mutation data will connect disrupted chain recognition to pathological phenotypes. Comparative analysis across chain types (K48, K63, linear, branched) will reveal principles of emergent specificity. This project requires expertise in ubiquitin biology, structural biology, computational chemistry, and proteomics—necessitating collaboration across specialized laboratories. The synthesis of structural, proteomic, and functional data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include models of emergent chain specificity, identification of key conformational features determining receptor selectivity, and principles for predicting ubiquitin signaling outcomes. Understanding the emergent ubiquitin code has implications for targeted protein degradation therapies. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent RNA Localization: Synthesizing Spatial Transcriptomics and RNA Structure Data to Model mRNA Targeting Networks
abstract: mRNA localization creates emergent spatial gene expression patterns through RNA-protein networks operating at the mesoscale—a phenomenon where RNA targeting achieves precision impossible from individual binding events. This synthesis project will decode emergent RNA localization by integrating spatial transcriptomics, structural biology, and RNA biology datasets. We will synthesize spatial transcriptomics from the Human Cell Atlas and published studies, RNA structure data from SHAPE-MaP experiments in public repositories, RNA-binding protein (RBP) interaction data from ENCODE eCLIP, and RBP localization from the Human Protein Atlas. The central question is: how do RBP networks create emergent mRNA targeting at the mesoscale (RNA granules of 100-1000 nm containing multiple mRNAs and RBPs) with subcellular precision? We hypothesize that emergent localization arises from combinatorial RBP binding, RNA secondary structure context, and phase separation into transport granules that integrate multiple weak targeting signals. Our computational approach combines machine learning to predict localization from sequence and structure features, network analysis of RBP-mRNA interactions, and spatial statistics to quantify localization precision. We will develop algorithms integrating RNA structure predictions with RBP binding sites to model targeting complexes. Integration with translation data will connect localization to local protein synthesis. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal conserved versus specialized emergent targeting mechanisms. This project demands expertise in RNA biology, spatial transcriptomics, structural biology, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of spatial, structural, and interaction data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent RNA localization, identification of key features determining targeting, and principles for engineering localized gene expression. Understanding emergent RNA targeting has implications for neurological diseases and mRNA therapeutics. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Mechanics of Bacterial Microcompartments: Synthesizing Structural and Metabolic Data to Model Encapsulated Pathway Efficiency
abstract: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) represent emergent metabolic organelles where protein shells encapsulate enzyme pathways, creating efficiency and selectivity impossible in the cytoplasm. This synthesis project will decode emergent BMC function by integrating structural biology, metabolomics, and systems biology datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of BMC shells and encapsulated enzymes, metabolomics from MetaboLights, enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, and genomic data on BMC operons from NCBI. The central question is: how does BMC shell architecture at the mesoscale (40-200 nm compartments) create emergent metabolic properties—enhanced pathway flux, toxic intermediate sequestration, and substrate selectivity—that free enzymes cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent efficiency arises from shell pore selectivity, enzyme co-localization effects, and internal environment optimization. Our computational approach combines finite element modeling of metabolite diffusion through BMC shells, kinetic modeling of encapsulated pathways, and machine learning to predict BMC function from shell composition. We will develop algorithms correlating shell protein properties with pore selectivity. Integration with fitness data from published studies will connect BMC organization to growth phenotypes. Comparative analysis across BMC types (carboxysomes, metabolosomes) will reveal shared principles of emergent encapsulated metabolism. This project requires expertise in BMC biology, structural biology, metabolic modeling, and biophysics—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, metabolic, and genomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent BMC efficiency, identification of key architectural features determining function, and principles for engineering synthetic compartments. Understanding emergent BMC function has implications for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent Receptor Clustering in Immune Synapses: Synthesizing Super-Resolution and Signaling Data to Model T Cell Activation Thresholds
abstract: T cell activation emerges from receptor clustering at immune synapses where mesoscale organization determines signaling thresholds—a phenomenon where spatial arrangement creates activation decisions impossible from receptor occupancy alone. This synthesis project will decode emergent T cell activation by integrating imaging, signaling, and structural datasets. We will synthesize super-resolution imaging from published studies and Image Data Resource, phosphoproteomics of TCR signaling from PRIDE, structural data from PDB on TCR complexes, and single-cell RNA-seq from the Human Cell Atlas. The central question is: how does receptor clustering at the mesoscale (100-500 nm microclusters) create emergent activation thresholds that determine T cell responses? We hypothesize that emergent thresholds arise from kinetic segregation of phosphatases, cooperative kinase recruitment, and feedback loops operating within receptor clusters. Our computational approach combines spatial stochastic simulations of TCR signaling, machine learning to predict activation from cluster properties, and network analysis of signaling cascades. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cluster properties across activation states. Integration with functional data will connect cluster organization to T cell fate decisions. Comparative analysis across T cell subsets will reveal how emergent thresholds adapt to different immune functions. This project demands expertise in T cell biology, super-resolution imaging, signaling, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent activation thresholds, identification of key cluster features determining T cell responses, and principles for modulating immune activation. Understanding emergent T cell activation has implications for immunotherapy and autoimmune diseases. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

title: Emergent DNA Repair Pathway Choice: Synthesizing Damage Proteomics and Chromatin Data to Model Repair Mechanism Selection
abstract: DNA repair pathway choice represents emergent decision-making where chromatin context, cell cycle stage, and damage characteristics collectively determine repair mechanism—a mesoscale phenomenon integrating multiple inputs into discrete outcomes. This synthesis project will decode emergent pathway choice by integrating damage proteomics, chromatin biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize DNA damage proteomics from PRIDE and published studies, ChIP-seq of repair factors from ENCODE, chromatin accessibility from ATAC-seq datasets, and cell cycle proteomics from published studies. The central question is: how do repair protein assemblies at damage sites (mesoscale foci of 100-1000 nm) create emergent pathway selection that individual protein-DNA interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent pathway choice arises from competitive recruitment kinetics, chromatin-mediated accessibility, and feedback loops that amplify initial pathway commitment. Our computational approach combines kinetic modeling of repair protein recruitment, machine learning to predict pathway choice from chromatin and damage features, and network analysis of repair factor interactions. We will develop algorithms integrating damage site proteomics with chromatin context to model pathway selection. Integration with mutation signature data from COSMIC will connect pathway choice to genomic outcomes. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal how emergent repair decisions adapt to different genomic contexts. This project requires expertise in DNA repair, chromatin biology, proteomics, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of damage, chromatin, and proteomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent pathway choice, identification of key features determining repair selection, and principles for modulating repair outcomes. Understanding emergent repair decisions has implications for cancer therapy and genome editing. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.
